speakeroldname: Hon. E. J. Benson (Minister of Finance):
subtopic: REPORT BY MINISTER ON INTERNATIONAL MEETINGS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker I would like to take this opportunity to report to the house very briefly on the international meetings which I attended recently.
The first of these was the annual meeting of commonwealth finance ministers held in London on September 25 and 26. It provided an occasion for an exchange of views within the Commonwealth on financial and economic questions of general interest. There was a general exchange of views on the world economic situation, including in particular matters of special interest to members of the sterling area and to the less developed Commonwealth countries.
The meeting was encouraged by the favourable prospects reported by the chancellor of the exchequer for a strengthening of the British balance of payments in the months ahead. The meeting also noted with satisfaction the arrangements concluded between overseas sterling area countries and Britain in connection with the facilities recently announced by the Bank for International Settlements. Under these arrangements $2 billion will be made available to Britain by the central banks of 12 countries, including Canada, to enhance the stability of sterling and of the international monetary situation. We also reviewed trends in development assistance. In this connection the meeting recognized the urgency and importance of the proposed replenishment of the resources of the International Development Association.
The matter of I.D.A. replenishment was also of special concern at the annual meetings of the boards of governors of the World Bank and the monetary fund which I attended last week in Washington. The I.D.A. is of great importance to developing countries which for balance of payments reasons are unable to finance all their capital requirements on terms provided by the World Bank. The
29180-54}
Canadian government has in the past actively supported early replenishment at a substantially higher level. At the recent meeting I reiterated that prompt completion of the necessary agreement for replenishment is essential if the World Bank group is to continue to play its full role in all parts of the underdeveloped world. As hon. members will be aware, the government has placed an estimates item before the house which would authorize the Canadian contribution to the proposed replenishment exercise.
This was the first annual meeting which Mr. McNamara attended in his new role as president of the World Bank. There is no doubt in my mind that he will provide the bank with vigorous and imaginative leadership. This is already reflected in the action he has taken with a view to expanding the resources and the scope of activities of the World Bank.
Mr. Speaker, I should like to use this opportunity to reply to the question asked by the Leader of the Opposition on October 1 in connection with my statement at the annual meeting of the I.M.F./I.B.R.D. board of governors.
I should make it clear first of all that this statement did not enunciate any new policies for the Canadian aid program. Speaking on behalf of the government of Canada I endorsed Mr. McNamara's plans and intentions for the World Bank which among other matters included three specific suggestions to deal with the problem of population growth in underdeveloped countries. These were as follows:
First: To let the developing nations know the extent to which rapid population growth slows down their potential development, and that, in consequence, the optimum employment of the world's scarce development funds requires attention to this problem.
Second: To seek opportunities to finance facilities required by our member countries to carry out family planning programs.
Third: To join with others in programs of research to determine the most effective methods of family planning and of national administration of population control programs.
With these three proposals for immediate action, I hope we may contribute to the success of the U.N. system which is already working in this field, and to the well-being of the developing nations.

This quotation from Mr. McNamara's speech at the annual meeting describes in full the proposed program of the bank in the field of population control. It should therefore be apparent that he did not envisage giving first preference for World Bank loans to countries which are willing to institute programs of population control. Further, in endorsing the course of action proposed by Mr. McNamara I was addressing myself exclusively to the activities of the World Bank and not those coming under Canada's bilateral aid program.
In contrast with last year's annual meeting in Rio de Janeiro, which focused heavily on developments in the I.M.F., this year's annual meeting was more directed to the World Bank group. The three outstanding issues in the I.M.F. on which most attention was focused were the status of the special drawing rights proposal, the progress made on last year's resolution calling for a possible I.M.F. and I.B.R.D. role in the stabilization of primary commodity prices, and gold.
On the first of these, the S.D.R. proposal, progress has been made since last year. It is now hoped that the I.M.F. will be in a position, if this is deemed desirable, to make an initial distribution of special drawing rights some time in 1969. To enable Canada to play its role in the I.M.F. this house will be asked at an early date to give its attention to a rather complex bill to amend the Bretton Woods Agreements Act.
On the commodity pricing question, the governors had before them the first part of a joint I.M.F./I.B.R.D. study providing a useful analysis of the problem. It was agreed that this study would be completed and that specific policy recommendations would be put forward by June 30 of next year.
As to gold, representatives of the countries, most directly concerned, including Canada, met during the week. At the conclusion of the meetings an agreed statement was issued. The relevant parts of the statement are as follows:
The governors unanimously agreed on a common position based on the Washington declaration ot March 17, 1968, regarding the disposal of newly mined gold. It has, however, not proved possible to reach agreement with South Africa at this meeting.

I should like to make one or two brief comments on the statement by the Minister of Finance, whom we are happy to see back in the house after an absence on official business. I cannot express quite as much satisfaction as he seems to feel with
regard to some of the arrangements made. I hope that the arrangement made with regard to the pound and the other transitional arrangements will in fact be carried out. But I suggest that while these may be the best arrangements which were possible in the circumstances, they still place a heavy burden on Britain in addition to the other burdens relating to the recovery of her economy.
I was disappointed, too, that more progress has not been made in the field of strengthening international currency arrangements. I am sure we are all delighted at the way in which the crisis of last winter has settled down. This is the proper time for an arrangement to be made, but progress has been very slow with regard to strengthening international currency arrangements.
So far as the arrangements regarding the World Bank and international aid generally are concerned, constructive proposals supported by this government certainly would have the support of this party. We believe the government of Canada ought to play an active role in supporting the World Bank and other international agencies interested in development. Certainly we would support any constructive measures in this regard.
But regard to the statement attributed to the minister concerning what Mr. McNamara may have said regarding priority being given to countries that adopt measures to control population, I may say that despite what the minister has said the situation is still a little confusing to me. It may very well be that this results from the necessary brevity of the minister's statement, and perhaps further discussion will clarify this matter.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to express my satisfaction with some of the things the minister has said, particularly the degree of co-operation that has taken place among the countries involved. I am glad to hear that he is working for the continuance of that co-operation, particularly in the area of making credit available to countries that need underpinning of their currency. We in Canada have every reason to realize how effective some of those measures can be, since we had to call on this type of assitance in the earlier part of the year. The very fact that nations can call upon each other for this type of help will have a tendan-cy to provide greater stability in international monetary circles.
I am, however, concerned about one thing, and in his statement the minister did not clear this up. This is the question of what

October 7, 1968

attitude Canada is going to take to the purchase of commodities from some of the underdeveloped nations, particularly Commonwealth nations. I must say that our record in this regard has not been particularly good. We have refused to make an agreement regarding sugar, which would have been most helpful to some of our neighbours and friends in the Commonwealth. While it has perhaps enriched some Canadians in a very minute way, it has gone a long way toward retarding the development and growth of nations that we seek to help.
In the long run, Mr. Speaker, gifts to underdeveloped nations, valuable as they may be, are not the real answer to solving the problems of the underdeveloped sections of the world. The real answer must be that we are prepared to trade with them and to buy those commodities they have available for export at fair prices. I am sure this is what they would want, and I am equally sure it is what Canada should do. Canada should take the lead in indicating its willingness to buy these commodities at fair prices so as to enable some of our friends in other parts of the world to improve their own conditions. We should not be impoverishing our friends in order to benefit ourselves.
I welcome the minister back, and I hope he will have something further to say to the house once the study on commodities has been completed.

subtopic: REPORT BY MINISTER ON INTERNATIONAL MEETINGS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the minister's statement deals mainly with the participation of Canada in the World Bank so that it may help further the development of countries in the whole world, mainly in Asia and Africa. The objectives of the Canadian government when participating in the activities of the World Bank are certainly commandable and the minister will recognize that the delegates have made a serious effort to adapt the financial situation to the needs of the those poverty stricken nations. As was was just mentioned by the hon. member who spoke before me, the question is not for Canada to provide almost unlimited funds in order to send them food, clothing, and so on; I think that the major part of Canada's participation should be to encourage those nations to produce certain commodities and to offer them for sale, in order to make their citizens responsible, because gifts alone are not the real answer to the problem.

Now, it is a little strange that the hon. minister should take part in the financial discussions of the World Bank and negotiate, for instance, the price of gold without reaching a conclusion which might help Canada to produce more gold at a reasonable price, in short at a better price than the one we receive at this time.
And while the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) is talking about helping poor countries, developing countries, our Canadian Prime Minister is on a trip out west where he preaches restraint and self-sacrifice or something like that.
We forget about education and the development of our natural resources but we are ready to share with other countries in the financing of the needs of developing countries. That is nonsense, Mr. Speaker, in my opinion, it would be advisable for the government to take its responsibilities, to act, not against the other countries, but first for our country, Canada, and then it can help developing countries.

maintopic: NIGERIA-MOTION FOR CONSIDERATION BY HOUSE COMMITTEE

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert L. Stanfield (Leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: NIGERIA-MOTION FOR CONSIDERATION BY HOUSE COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, pursuant to standing order 42 I seek the unanimous consent of the house to permit me to move a motion which, because of its urgent and pressing necessity, should not be delayed by the 48 hour notice rule. I recognize that standing order 42 has not often been invoked in this house, but I think the house will agree that the standing order was framed to cover just the sort of emergency which faces us today.
Standing order 42 reads as follows:
A motion may, in case of urgent and pressing necessity previously explained by the mover, be made by unanimous consent of the house without notice having been given under standing order 4i.
That is the rule. Under standing order 42 I am entitled to explain the urgent and pressing necessity of this motion, and I simply wish to take a few moments to do so. My motion seeks to have the house order the standing committee on external affairs and national defence the members of which will be named later today, to meet not later than tomorrow morning in order to discuss and hear evidence on the tragedy in Biafra and, hopefully, to make recommendations which will enable Canada to take the most effective part possible in meeting both a humanitarian and political challenge.
The motion I seek to move sets out terms of reference sufficiently broad which I believe will commend themselves to members of this house. I am sure there is no doubt in the mind of any hon. member as to the urgent and pressing necessity of obtaining further information on this tragedy. It has been estimated that at least 6,000 civilians are dying of starvation every day in Biafra.
Although we have not officially received the report of the official observer group, we have read in the press that that group asserts there is ho evidence of genocide and that food supplies for civilians are adequate in Biafra. We must find out what parts of Nigeria this observer group visited and under what conditions. The house is already aware that two of its hon. members, the hon. member for Egmont (Mr. MacDonald) and the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin), have just returned from visiting those lands which are still in Biafran hands. I doubt whether in the history of Canada there has ever been a human tragedy so far from our shores which has had such a powerful effect on the consciences of Canadians. The Prime Minister
[Mr. Speaker.)
is well aware of the interest many Canadians take in this matter and of the depth of feeling that exists.
I am therefore asking the house to proceed under standing order 42, and we wish to emphasize that our primary concern is not to engage in debate at this point but rather to obtain as much factual information as possible. To that end the committee on external affairs and national defence ought to hear evidence and bring in recommendations which will enable the government and this house to take effective and immediate action.
It will be seen from the motion that while the hon. member for Greenwood and the hon. member for Egmont are to be invited to report their observations to the committee, it will be open to the committee to hear evidence from other sources in a position to give evidence on the situation in Biafra.
I therefore seek the unanimous consent of the house to move the following motion, seconded by my hon. friend from Peace River:
That It be resolved by the House of Commons that it is urgent and expedient that it order the standing committee on external affairs and national defence, to be named later this day, to convene not later than 11:00 a.m. Tuesday, October 8 to hear evidence on (1) the report of the official observer group on which Canada has a member, of the conduct of federal troops in the prosecution of the war in Nigeria, (2) the reported famine conditions in that country, and to invite Andrew Brewin, M.P. (Greenwood) and David MacDonald, M.P. (Egmont) to report their observations on the conditions of the civilian population in Nigeria, and to report its findings to this house with all convenient speed.
I have not in the motion set a time limit for the committee but I would be disappointed, should the house adopt this resolution, if the committee did not report back to the house within one week.

May I express my appreciation to the House of Commons for giving unanimous consent. Perhaps I should add one further word in requesting the house to adopt this resolution, now that consent has been obtained. There has, I think, been a considerable lack of hard information concerning the suffering and strife in Nigeria and Biafra, but it does not seem to be disputed that large numbers of persons are dying each day. There are apparently conflicting reports from our observers in Nigeria and from reporters and members of this house who have visited Biafra. The committee which it is proposed to establish will be able to hold hearings and judge, with respect to General Milroy's travels in Nigeria for instance, how much freedom of movement was accorded to him, and how realistic are the charges that he was able to see only model villages. In effect the committee will be able to judge what weight should be given to the evidence of the observers.
[DOT] (3:00 p.m.)
It is to be hoped that a similar close scrutiny will be given to the reports of other witnesses the committee will hear. In establishing this committee the house will learn where it is that people are starving if not in the areas visited by General Milroy. Through this committee we will be able to establish what form our relief ought to take; should we continue to concentrate on sending food, or should we be sending planes and medicines as well?
This committee should also be able to establish which relief agencies are best able to get the food to the starving. And by establishing the committee the government and this house will be able in short order to have the facts at its and our disposal, facts needed to make decisions which will lead to effective relief efforts by our country.

maintopic: NIGERIA-MOTION FOR CONSIDERATION BY HOUSE COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we on the government side will be very happy to give unanimous consent to this motion, because we are interested in the obtaining of as much information on this situation as is possible, not only from members of the House of Commons but also from the Canadian public. We feel it is important not only to have information, but to understand also all the difficulties in international law and usage, in bringing about a proper solution to this problem.

Motion to Consider Nigerian Situation
I do not want to make this a long debate. I am prepared to say now that if this is the best way of doing it then we give unanimous consent to the introduction of the motion. I should like to say, however, that it was our intention to set up the committees of the house as soon as we had the names for the various committees from the opposition parties. There has been a bit of delay, though not on this committee. This committee can be set up now. Nevertheless, we do want to set up all the committees as soon as possible.
Our opinion is that if this standing committee of the house could be set up this afternoon we would be prepared to refer the estimates to it this afternoon or tomorrow, sir, and of course all aspects of this matter could be brought out before that committee. We are a little afraid, however, that the terms of the present motion, although certainly valuable and acceptable to our side, may perhaps be a bit too restrictive.
There is the question of the reported famine, but we feel it might be important to have any evidence available on the accusation of genocide as well. We feel that that is a very relevant part of the whole discussion because obviously the beleaguered parts of Nigeria are being pressured into some kind of submission either by force of arms or by force of hunger. The relevant question of whether this is going to be followed by genocide is something I think the committee would be interested in hearing about. The observers sent by our country and other countries have no evidence of that, but it would be interesting to learn if they are allowed to travel to other parts of Nigeria.
The Secretary of State for External Affairs is at present trying to ensure that the Canadian observer will be allowed to travel as widely as possible and to report as usefully as possible. The government did make the point earlier, when it was invited to send an observer to Nigeria, that it would not accept the invitation right away because we wanted some guarantee that our observer would not merely be in a position to whitewash the Nigerian government. We wanted to make sure that he would be there to obtain an impartial opinion and make impartial observations, and it was after getting a beginning to some guarantee on that point that we named our observer.
I make the point that we will accept this motion, but we feel the proper approach would be not only to hear these gentlemen but also to hear other people the committee

Motion to Consider Nigerian Situation might want to listen to, including the Secretary of State for External Affairs when he comes back from New York. He has been down there holding a great number of discussions on the Biafran question. He is trying to advance the cause of humanity as much as he can, and it would be an advantage to have the committee hear him as soon as he comes back from the United Nations.
For these reasons, Mr. Speaker, we feel the alternative would be not to accept this motion but to have the standing committee seized right away, tomorrow, with the estimates of the Department of External Affairs and then be free to deal with all aspects of this question. I do not want to press this point, though other members of the house and of our party may want to follow up that suggestion.

maintopic: NIGERIA-MOTION FOR CONSIDERATION BY HOUSE COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on behalf of my colleagues and myself I welcome the motion, and as I informed the Leader of the Opposition we are very pleased that he is putting it forward. May I say to the right hon. Prime Minister, Mr. Speaker, on the last point he put forward, that he can accomplish both the objectives he has stated.
I suggest that the value of the motion is that it gives the subject matter of the motion priority when the committee assembles tomorrow, and I point out that the motion asks that the committee assemble tomorrow to deal with this matter. If the government will carry out the Prime Minister's suggestion, as I hope it will today, and (a) appoint the committee of external affairs and national defence and (b) refer the estimates to that committee, then, of course, the committee will be able to make any other inquiry relating to the situation in Biafra or any other situation. It will then have the authority not only of the terms of reference of this motion but also the general authority under the estimates to make the fullest possible inquiry.
Therefore on our behalf, and I am sure on behalf of other members of the opposition, I would agree that if the Prime Minister accepts the motion, as he has suggested he will despite his doubts, and in order to deal with the matter that concerns him at the same time the committee is appointed by the house have the estimates referred to that committee, then the widest possible inquiry will be available to it.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I want to make this point also, and I want to make it as strongly
(Mr. Trudeau.]
as I can. I am in favour of this subject going to the committee, but it is obvious that no matter how expeditiously the committee may handle the matter there will necessarily be some time consumed, maybe a week, maybe two weeks, and maybe as long as three weeks, before the committee is able to bring any recommendations to the house. I think it would be a dereliction of our duty as a parliament, a dereliction of the government's duty and of the duty of the people of Canada, if we waited until that committee reported before taking any action. I urge the government and the house not to permit the reference to the committee to be an excuse for inaction for the next one, two or three weeks.
I know, as all hon. members of the house know, that our colleagues the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin) and the hon. member for Egmont (Mr. MacDonald), had an audience with the Prime Minister today, and that they are pursuing certain suggestions that were discussed with him. I see no reason why some of the actions that are urgently needed, such as the lending of Hercules aircraft and similar actions, should be delayed pending the results of the inquiry and report of the committee. I think it is important to emphasize this because it is all too easy to appoint a committee to make inquiries and then sit back until the committee reports. This situation is too urgent for that.
May I also point out that events in Nigeria-Biafra are moving rapidly. At one point it looked as if federal forces were going to capture all of Biafra. At the moment it looks as if the Biafran forces have been able to set back the advance of the Nigerian forces, but one never knows what will happen in the next few days and the problem of relief, of additional transport planes, is too urgent to wait upon the deliberations of the committee.
I think I also agree with the right hon. Prime Minister that the Secretary of State for External Affairs and the responsible officials of his department ought to be heard by the committee to explain more fully than he has been able to explain to this house the reason for certain attitudes of the government during the last few weeks, the details of which I need not go into. I think we ought to know more than we do now as to why the government has taken a position against certain actions that might have been taken before
now.
October 7, 1968

[DOT] (3:10 p.m.)
I certainly agree that the whole problem, and whether the fear of the Biafrans that the federal government is out to annihilate many of the Biafran people has any validity should be considered. Therefore in summary I support wholeheartedly on behalf of my colleagues the motion before this house, with the reservation that neither the government nor this house ought to permit the appointment of the committee to delay any action which can and should be taken as soon as possible to assist this desperate situation of the Biafran people.

maintopic: NIGERIA-MOTION FOR CONSIDERATION BY HOUSE COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my colleagues and I also agree with the Leader of the Official Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) that it is urgent and expedient that the standing committee on external affairs and national defence convene as soon as possible to discuss the situation in Nigeria.
I think that all members should commend the hon. members for Greenwood and Egmont (Messrs. Brewin and MacDonald) for their initiative in going there and observing what was going on, so that the Canadian government might be better informed on the situation now existing in Nigeria. According to the news published in newspapers, or broadcast on radio and television, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) tells us over and over again that Nigeria is a friendly nation and that we must avoid taking initiatives that could be prejudicial to this friendship between Nigeria and Canada. However, perhaps there is a difference between that and knowing and saying exactly what is happening in Nigeria. Anyone can have a perfectly proper person for a friend who, for some reason or other, suddenly becomes a gangster of sorts, he is then no longer your friend.
For example, when we learn that Red Cross people are shot like dogs by Nigerian troops or people attached to them, in my opinion we have a duty to take a stand, not two or three weeks hence but immediately. When we read in the press that civilians, children and mothers of families are starving, that they are worse off than animals, I say that there is a limit to abuse, even though Nigeria is a friend of Canada. It is important, therefore, that the committee should meet to hear especially the two members who have come back from Nigeria, and to know exactly what the living conditions of the civilian populations are in Nigeria.

Motion to Consider Nigerian Situation
We, therefore, support with enthusiasm the motion of the Leader of the Official Opposition to the effect that the standing committee should meet as soon as possible. However, as the honourable member for York South (Mr. Lewis) said a while ago, let us not wait two or three weeks or even a month before getting a report and knowing what position to adopt, and what action to take in order to help and protect the unfortunate peoples of Nigeria.

Mr. Speaker, as the Prime Minister has already pointed out to the house the terms of the motion are rather restricted in the sense that they confine themselves to the report in which General Milroy participated, and the expedition of the hon. member for Greenwood and the hon. member for Egmont. As the Prime Minister indicated, it would be desirable that not only the reports of these two different groups but events in Nigeria generally should be considered by the standing committee on external affairs and national defence.
Therefore I should like to indicate it is my intention after this motion is adopted to move under the standing orders that the estimates of the Department of External Affairs for 1968-69 be referred to the standing committee later this day, when I receive the nominations of all hon. gentlemen opposite to that committee. In that way I hope the estimates and this particular resolution can be considered together so that all the events taking place in Nigeria and particularly in that part called Biafra can be looked into by the committee at an early date.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: ADMIRALTY COURT
speechtext:
1.	The Admiralty Act, Chapter 1, Revised Statutes of Canada, 1952, provides that the Exchequer Court of Canada shall continue to be a Court of Admiralty and to be as such a court of record and shall have and exercise on its Admiralty side general jurisdiction in Admiralty and that the President and the Puisne Judges of the Exchequer Court shall have and exercise throughout Canada the Admiralty jurisdiction of the Court. The Act also provides for the appointment by the Governor General, from time to time, of any judge of a superior or county court, or any

barrister of not less than ten years standing, to be a District Judge in Admiralty of the Exchequer Court in and for the Admiralty District. There are such District Judges in each of the Admiralty Districts of Quebec, Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Prince Edward Island, British Columbia, Ontario, Newfoundland and Manitoba. In addition, the Act provides that a District Judge in Admiralty, or, if he is incapacitated, a Judge of the Exchequer Court, may, from time to time, with the approval of the Governor in Council, appoint a Deputy Judge having the qualifications of a District Judge, having all such jurisdiction, powers and authority as are possessed by the District Judge. The Governor in Council may also, from time to time, appoint for any district, or portion of an Admiralty District, a Surrogate Judge or Judges.
2.	There are registries in Toronto, Ontario; Quebec and Montreal in the Province of Quebec; Halifax, Nova Scotia; Saint John, New Brunswick; Victoria, and Vancouver in the Province of British Columbia; Charlottetown, Prince Edward Island and Winnipeg, Manitoba.

USE OF HOVERCRAFT IN MARITIMES FERRY SERVICES
speechtext:
1.	Has the government made any study of the possible feasibility of augmenting the Borden-Cape Tormentine ferry service and/or the Wood Islands-Caribou ferry service with the SRN 4-type Hovercraft, which will carry over 30 automobiles and 250 passengers at speeds up to 35 m.p.h., and which was to go into use on the Dover-Boulogne crosschannel route on August 1, 1968?
2.	If such a study has been made, what were the conclusions arrived at?

subtopic: USE OF HOVERCRAFT IN MARITIMES FERRY SERVICES
speechtext:
1.	Yes.
2.	The government, as part of its policy to assess and monitor the applicability of air cushion vehicles in Canada, has in co-operation with industry conducted a series of studies to enhance the area of knowledge relating to this new form of transport. This process has involved the conduct of operational tests in the north to assess the problems associated with operations under severe winter conditions, the employment of consultants to investigate and report on the market potential for air cushion vehicles in Canada and to prepare recommendations on the suitable future development of vehicles, and a study within the Department of Transport to assess the operational and economic characteristics of existing craft and to test their applicability to specific routes in Canada.
As part of this activity, studies have been conducted jointly by the staff of the Department of Transport and of British Hovercraft Corporation to investigate the problems associated with the operation of either the existing or specially developed SRN-4 Hovercraft for the Prince Edward Island ferry system. These studies are being actively continued and consideration is being given to the possibility of conducting trials in the Northumberland strait. I shall inform the house if and when an acceptable proposal has been worked out.
The results of studies conducted so far indicate that the cost of transporting cars between Borden and Tormentine by an SRN-4 is considerably more expensive than by the use of modern ferries. On the other hand, the amphibious quality of the SRN-4 may make it possible to conduct fast and regular services in the strait during the winter season when existing ferry services are hampered. The tests which are under study, will give better information on the general suitability of the SRN-4 for service not only in the Northumberland strait but also on other routes in eastern Canada.

speechtext:
1.	Is it the intention of the government to continue to allow the importation into Canada of

Russian construction equipment similar to that recently imported by Znider Bros. Construction Equipment Ltd. of Etobicoke?
2.	What was the basis of evaluation and the rate of duty applied to the above equipment?
3.	How does this compare to the method of evaluation and application of duty in the case of "Most Favoured Nations"?
4.	Did the Russian Government subsidize in any way the manufacture of the equipment, the application of the equipment in Canada and/or the rental being paid to Znider Bros, who are alleged to be the importers and owners of the Halegate Equipment Co. of Britain?

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean-Pierre Cote (Minister of National Revenue):
subtopic: IMPORTATION OF RUSSIAN CONSTRUCTION EQUIPMENT
speechtext:
1. The Canadian-Soviet
trade agreement provides that goods of U.S.S.R. origin are entitled to most favoured nation tariff treatment. The trade agreement was extended in 1966 for a period of three years and governs the tariff treatment accorded to construction equipment.
2.	The values declared on the customs invoices were used in determining the value for duty. Under the most favoured nation tariff agreement, the bulldozers, tractors and combines, which have been imported, are entitled to entry free of duty, the excavators were entered at the 15 per cent rate of duty. Off-highway trucks, which have not at this time been entered for consumption, are subject to a 10 per cent duty rate.
3.	The valuation for customs purposes of goods imported into Canada is not dependent upon the tariff treatment accorded the country of export. Under the valuation provisions of the Customs Act, goods are normally valued at the higher of the fair market value or the selling price to the purchaser in Canada. This procedure was followed in this case.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have not read any report beyond that which has been published in the newspapers, but I think I may assume that the department has also received the report.

subsubtopic: NIGERIA-INQUIRY AS TO REPORT OF CANADIAN OBSERVER
speechtext:

upon our good relations with other countries, this can be done. I would not publish it without their permission. I do not think any of these "ifs" should materialize. I undertake to report as soon as I have read it.

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: NIGERIA-INQUIRY AS TO REPORT OF CANADIAN OBSERVER
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, relating to the same subject, I should like to ask the Prime Minister whether he has received a cable from the Biafran head of state, sent to the president of the general assembly of the United Nations, pleading that appropriate action be taken at the United Nations to deal with what are alleged to be acts of genocide against the people of Biafra. If so, what reply has the Prime Minister made to the cable, and what action is the Canadian government proposing to take in respect of it?

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: NIGERIA-INQUIRY AS TO REPORT OF CANADIAN OBSERVER
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have not yet seen the cable; therefore I have not replied to it. With regard to action, I repeat that the Secretary of State for External Affairs is in the process, and has been for several days now, of consulting with members of the United Nations and with the Secretary General to see whether any such action can be initiated in the United Nations.

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: NIGERIA-INQUIRY AS TO REPORT OF CANADIAN OBSERVER
speechtext: A supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: NIGERIA-INQUIRY AS TO REPORT OF CANADIAN OBSERVER

speechtext: A further supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: NIGERIA-INQUIRY AS TO REPORT OF CANADIAN OBSERVER
speechtext:
Yes, Mr. Speaker.

subsubtopic: NIGERIA-INQUIRY AS TO REPORT OF CANADIAN OBSERVER
speechtext: A supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. Is one of the questions being taken up at the United Nations by the Secretary of State for External Affairs the supplying of arms by Britain, the U.S.S.R. and France to the participants in this fratricidal war?

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: NIGERIA-INQUIRY AS TO REPORT OF CANADIAN OBSERVER
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I do not believe that is the object of direct representations. The position of this government, of course, is that we are not supplying arms to either side and we think this should be the position of other friendly powers. I am prepared to say that publicly. But I do not think we should believe our consciences will be eased by telling other people what they should do. I believe the government of the United Kingdom is under pressure from its own people to reconsider these policies, and I regard that that is the proper point of pressure to be brought to bear.

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: NIGERIA-INQUIRY AS TO REPORT OF CANADIAN OBSERVER

There has been some question whether this matter should be referred to a standing committee. I for one am not urging that this be done, but if it is not done there are a number of questions that the minister on behalf of the government must be prepared to answer before the bill is put through all stages.
From what I know of this project and from what the minister has said, it appears at first blush to be a program which will have beneficial effects for the country. It will probably add substantially to the gross national product and will result in the employment of a number of people and the production of a commodity desired in the world and for which Canada has the opportunity of establishing an export market. Nevertheless, the legislation involves the expenditure of $10 million of the taxpayers' money.
One advantage of sending a bill of this kind to a standing committee, as was done by the Conservative government in 1960 and 1961 with two major construction programs, one involving the Mattagami railway in the province of Quebec and the other the Great Slave Lake railway, is that it provides an opportunity for members of the standing committee to ask a series of questions with regard to the cost, traffic guarantees, the amount of traffic that will be generated, and whether the freight changes will be agreed rates. All of these questions are very pertinent. In authorizing this measure we are acting for the taxpayers of Canada, because this $10 million will come from the consolidated revenue fund. Therefore I will put these questions to the minister now. He may not be able to answer them specifically, but I suggest that he at least give us a guarantee that when the bill is considered by the committee of the whole house, if that is the way the house decides to proceed, the minister will have available to him his officials armed with the facts.
We want to know what will be the cost per mile of this railway. We have been told in general what traffic will be generated, but we should like to know the gross amount of the traffic and what guarantees there are. We also

want to know over what period of years this traffic will be maintained. We should like to know what guarantees there will be as to quantity and yearly shipment. We should like to know about the freight rate and compare it with the rates in other comparable operations. Will it in fact be an agreed rate?
We should also like to know whether there is any overriding guarantee as to the total minimum traffic, and over what period of years. We should like some information as to the amount of employment generated both at the plants involved and also on the railway itself. We should like to know what will be the value of the production planned and to what extent it will result in an increase in the gross national product.
In his speech at the resolution stage the minister said, as reported on page 638 of Hansard:
The management of the C.N.R. has informed me that by means of traffic guarantee contracts made with the two companies whose names I have mentioned, the C.N.R. is assured that the products of these plants will be shipped over the new lines and over the other lines of the C.N.R. in such volumes that the revenue therefrom will support all the costs of the lines-
I do not doubt that, Mr. Speaker, but I think hon. members are entitled to have a look at these agreements and know what is involved in them. There have been eases in the past where railroads have indicated what in their view would be the means of raising revenue from freight to cover the cost of building a new line and subsequently they have been disappointed.
I suggest these are facts to which we are entitled. Certainly in the case of both railway projects to which I referred the standing committee made a careful and detailed study. Questions were asked of the C.N.R. officials and of the minister. When the time came that the committee was ready to make its recommendations to the house the committee was satisfied, after a full and searching inquiry, that the project was in fact one which deserved the support of the house and all the facts were before the house.
I do not doubt that this will be the case now, and I appreciate, of course, the need for haste. I understand that time is of the essence and that there is a need to get the project launched and construction started as early as possible this fall. Although the time spent in sending the matter to the standing committee and then waiting for it to come back here may seriously retard the commencement of the construction and completion of the railway,

Mr. Speaker, on a point of order, I realize that if the minister speaks now he will close the debate. While we are dealing with Bill No. C-109 I feel I have the opportunity to bring to the attention of the house and the minister a matter which has been before us for quite some time now.
In Bill No. C-109 we are being asked to authorize the Canadian National Railways to expend a certain amount of money to construct a line of railway in northern Alberta. No one is objecting to this provision. Some years ago a bill similar in intent and purpose to the one now before the house was introduced and passed, and as a result the Canadian National called for tenders for the building of the Great Slave Lake railway. For the past two and a half to three years hon. members on this side and on the government side of the house have asked the Minister of Transport to look into the matter of improper tendering with respect to that railway. Allegations have been made that serious errors in the enforcement of the terms of contract were made by the Canadian National, as a result of which some contracting firms engaged in building that railway for the C.N.R. went into bankruptcy.
I realize that under the rules there are limitations on how deeply I can go into the construction of the Great Slave Lake railway by the Canadian National. To keep the matter brief and to the point, I and other hon. members of this house do not feel under any obligation at this time to vote additional sums of money under this bill for a new line to be built by the Canadian National until we receive some answers from the Minister of Transport on a matter which he says he has been studying for some time.
About March 20 last I asked the Minister of Transport whether he had received any claims accompanied by briefs from those construction firms that had been engaged in the construction of the Great Slave Lake railway. The minister said he had received claims and briefs, that they were complex and voluminous and that he needed time to study them. Several months have passed since then and in the meantime some firms have been forced into receivership and bankruptcy. Some were forced into bankruptcy before the matter was brought to the minister's attention by members of this house. Since that time I understand one or two other firms engaged in the construction have also been forced into receivership.

Lest the Acting Minister of Transport tries to say that those contractors who worked for the Canadian National ought to have exercised their rights and brought their claims before the courts, I wish to say that all possible legal avenues have been exhausted. The situation is very like the one that existed in the early 1960's when the northern Ontario pipe line was constructed. At that time five or six construction firms were placed in a precarious and untenable financial position, not through their own fault but as a result of sloppy specifications which were given for job tenders by the crown corporation involved. As a consequence a number of firms which lost heavily in the construction of the pipe line made claims for compensation. I do not care whether one considers an extra payment an ex gratia payment from the crown. The fact is that the contracting firms I have just referred to had no alternative but to make a special claim for payment. The matter was brought before the Treasury Board in 1961, I believe.

-the construction of a line of railway in the Province of Alberta by Canadian National Railway Company from the vicinity of Windfall on the Windfall Extension to the Sangudo Subdivision of the Canadian National Railway in a westerly direction-
This deals with the construction of a 60 mile line at an average cost of $174,000 per mile or at an estimated cost of $10,435,000 according to the schedule. The bill mentions that the Minister of Finance will have authority to advance money, to make loans available, not in excess of $12 million. In addition, the contract will be awarded by tenders. This is still no guarantee that the contract will go to the lowest bidder. The contractor's solvency will probably be considered. Should a tender be a little higher than the lowest one and should the contractor be more solvent, the government reserves the right to choose the tenderer it pleases.
Mr. Speaker, 1 wish to call the minister's attention to this point. At a time when the C.N.R. and the C.P.R. are forced to abandon some railway lines, as is now the case with the Ontario Northland Railway in northwestern Quebec and northeastern Ontario, has the government studied closely whether it would be economic to build a railway line in Alberta? Will it still be used in five or ten years, in view of the fact that the trucking industry could undoubtedly meet the needs of the area which will be served by the C.N.R.?
If the operation of this railway line becomes less economic year after year, I wonder whether, at a time when credit is so hard to get, at a time when it is so difficult to undertake constructions that would be useful to our people, the government would not be well-advised to consider thoroughly that matter and the situation in that area of Alberta. The fact is not that we object to the construction of a railway line, far from it. However, if the trucking industry should meet the requirements in that area of Alberta, I cannot see why the government would assume the responsibility of constructing such a line which would finally cost $10 to $12 million.
If we follow the example of the National Arts Centre in Ottawa, the construction of that railroad could well cost $35 million. We should, therefore, examine very carefully that proposal for the construction of a railroad in Alberta. We should ascertain whether that project will be profitable. Will the Canadian National make a profit by operating that railroad? If it is proved that it will, then we will not oppose it. On the other hand, if it is doubtful, in view of the fact that people turn more and more to trucking instead of railroads, then I feel that the Canadian government is not authorized to spend from $10 to $12 million for the construction of a railroad that will be abandoned within a few years.
These then, Mr. Speaker, are a few of the impressions I had on reading Bill No. C-109. I say again that we have no objection to the

Mr. Speaker, I have been very interested lately in the subject of government contracts and I was particularly interested in what was said by the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Schrey-er) regarding the contracts which will be let following the passage of this legislation. The conditions and guarantees for which provision is made when such contracts are entered into are diverse in nature, as I have found from recent experience.
I should like to refer to two provisions which in my opinion the bill before us should contain. One relates to the point made by the hon. member for Selkirk. In providing a guarantee of financial assistance to the railway company the government should retain a certain amount of power to prescribe the conditions of contracts to be let under this arrangement. The situation which developed in connection with the Great Slave Lake railway could easily develop in the case of the line we are now considering. The point raised by the hon. member for Temiscamingue (Mr. Caouette) was that the present arrangement might result in expenditures much greater than those anticipated in the bill we are now considering.
The failure in the past of the government and of crown corporations to make adequate provisions for the protection of those engaged in the construction of public works is much to be regretted. The powers of the federal government are rarely sufficient to make sure that tendering procedures are effective. I might refer to a case of which you, Mr. Speaker, have intimate knowledge. In the reconstruction of the west block, for instance, there turned out to be no relationship between the original tenders and the final amount paid in connection with every aspect of the contract. This is true in respect of many government contracts, if not of most of them. Yet this bill seems to contain no means of protection against the type of possibility which is bothering the hon. member for Temiscamingue in relation to the national arts centre.
In my own area we have encountered a great deal of difficulty this year in connection with a government contract. In this case peo-

pie in one province are employed as prime contractors to carry out public works in another province. I realize that the employment picture of Ontario Hydro has no relation to the present bill except in the sense that employment is affected, but it is relevant to point out that when the Quebec provincial government lets a contract it specifies that the people employed must come from that province. Not only the contractors but the workmen employed must come from that province. This affects Ontario workers. People living near the border, unable to obtain employment in connection with Quebec Hydro projects, have even found themselves denied employment in Ontario because they lack the experience which Quebec workers have gained while employed in both provinces.
I raise this point because I think it is time we took advantage of experience gained in letting contracts in northern areas where local inhabitants must be given preference in terms of employment. I believe a similar provision should be written into the bill before us because I see no other way in which this result can be achieved in the absence of general or overriding legislation on this point. I recall legislation brought in by a former minister of northern affairs in which there was a clause to the effect that the native population should be given preference in terms of employment whenever they were available and suitable. If we cannot have over-all legislation providing for this type of employment then it should be a factor in this bill. I recommend to the minister sponsoring the bill that a clause be written into it providing for a 10 per cent local employment factor, which in turn will be inserted in the tenders issued to the contractors.

Does the minister know whether there is any requirement in the tenders and subsequent contracts signed by contractors calling for a minimum standard of eating, sleeping and recreational facilities to be provided by the contractor? If this is not the case, will the minister take up this matter with Canadian National?
We run into situations where there are a large number of wildcat strikes. Some are very close to the minister's area and some are very close to the area of the hon. member for Saskatoon-Humboldt. This is quite general during the construction stage in such large operations. I think there should be some requirement in the contracts whereby contractors must provide a good standard of eating, sleeping and recreational facilities because in this part of Canada-the hon. member for Peace River could tell us better- I suspect there are absolutely no such facilities available off the scene of construction.
I hope the minister will remind Canadian National that certainly in some cases the calibre and quality of the facilities provided for their employees are most inadequate. Some of the old boarding cars that have been used for extra gangs you and I, Mr. Chairman, would not keep cattle in. If these people are to be 200, 300 or 400 miles away from any large settlement or centre, they must have decent living, eating and sleeping facilities. I hope the acting minister will pass this on to Canadian National and assure them that this matter will be watched.

Mr. Chairman, I realize lull well that the Acting Minister of Transport said the C.N.R. would like to get going on the construction of this line of railway in northern Alberta just as quickly as possible. Like other hon. members, I would like to see this public work completed. It would contribute greatly to the economic development of this part of the country. But it is not as simple as that. The Canadian National may be in a hurry now but it apparently is not always in a hurry when it comes to dealing with problems which come before it.
I say again to the Acting Minister of Transport that since he has become involved in this department and is helping the minister to deal with the problems in this portfolio, he should ask for the files of the C.N.R. regarding the construction of the Great Slave Lake, Pine Point railway. Some construction firms, Hatch Construction, Pete Rohl Construction, Ginter Construction, Krywa Brothers Construction, Lucas Construction and others, have been put into bankruptcy because of clause 16 of the form of contract.
This form of contract has been used by the C.N.R. in reaching agreement with construction firms which undertake to build roadbeds for them. I do not know how long clause 16 has been a normal part of the form of contract used by the C.N.R. Rumour has it that after many years and in fact decades this clause has been dropped. I wish I knew for sure. I would certainly hesitate to vote sums of money to be provided to the C.N.R., which will be used to pay contractors for the building of this new railway, if I felt there was a chance that clause 16 was still in the form of contract.
Clause 16 was in the form of contract in the case of the construction of Great Slave Lake railway. This clause was enforced in such an unconscionable way that it contributed directly to the bankruptcy of four or five road construction companies. The acting minister must, and I am sure he will, avail himself of all the briefs, printed documents and material which have accumulated in the office of the Minister of Transport. I am sure the acting minister will want to look at this material in detail to see what course of action can now be followed in order to redress the grievances of these people. There is no use talking about their right of access to the courts. In some cases justice, unfortunately, still is not obtainable without money with which to hire legal counsel, etc.

Most of these construction companies were bonded. In one, two or three instances the bonding companies exerted such pressure on the contractors that they forced them to sign off. The harshness of it is that the contractors simply had no legal recourse but morally, in terms of what was right and ethical, I am satisfied they have an iron-clad case. I am just about sick of the Minister of Transport taking seven months to make up his mind whether he thinks they have a case.

I have some fairly harsh thoughts about Canadian National in another context and in relationship to some other forms of activity. For a publicly owned company I do not believe it to be the least bit progressive, desirous of advancing the interests of the economy, or anything of that sort. It is, rather, a sort of ultraconservative, status quo type of corporate structure that can become pretty callous and have a great deal of disregard for the well-being of people.
Apart from that, there is a factor in our economic life I do not particularly like, which I am sure many other hon. members do not like either, that may well come into play with respect to any of the contractors the C.N. engages to do any of its work. The situation to which I refer would arise from the type of collective agreement between any one union

and the company containing the so-called closed shop principle. Incidentally, this is a principle with which I do not agree, particularly because it militates against the employment of people within the locale where the work is taking place. It has been my experience in the past that the situation can arise where a union having its local headquarters in one of the major cities within a province will have a collective agreement with an employer who has a contract to perform construction work 500, 800 or 1,000 miles distant from the headquarters of the union and in some cases from the headquarters of the construction company itself. Because of the closed shop principle contained in such collective agreements under which a person wishing to be employed on the job must first be a member of the union, we find that construction crews from the cities go out into the hinterland or into rural areas to perform the construction work. People in the local area, regardless of the fact that they may be perfectly qualified tradesmen in the particular occupation that is involved, are precluded from having any opportunity to become gainfully employed on that construction project because there is a collective agreement which works against them.

I have just been consulting with some of my colleagues and we find we do not have at hand what we would consider appropriate wording by way of an amendment to guarantee the opportunity of employment to people in the area where the construction will take place. subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE ADDITIONAL JUDGES FOR ONTARIO AND QUEBEC
speechtext:
that the house go into committee to consider the following resolution:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to amend the Judges Act to provide salaries for three additional Ontario County Court judges and eleven additional Quebec Superior Court judges.

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE ADDITIONAL JUDGES FOR ONTARIO AND QUEBEC
speechtext:
As hon. members will note, Mr. Chairman, the resolution provides for three additional Ontario County Court judges and 11 additional Quebec Superior Court judges. Perhaps I might address a few remarks to the second of the

two basic proposals involved in the resolution. I point out that the necessity for the 11 additional Quebec Superior Court judges, which hon. members will at once recognize as an important addition to the judicial force of that particular province, has been the direct result of the decision by the province of Quebec to take advantage of legislation passed at the last session to amend the divorce law.
If hon. members will recall, at the time that bill was before the house it was not anticipated that Quebec would, at least in the current year, take advantage of the opportunity to assume jurisdiction over divorce. It was assumed that the province would continue to use proceedings which had been established over the years for the granting of divorce by parliament. However, late in the month of June the Quebec government made a decision to take advantage of the provisions in that divorce measure which made it possibel for that province, as well as the province of Newfoundland, to assume jurisdiction over divorce. The necessity arises, therefore, to provide for additional judges so that the courts may exercise jurisdiction in this area. This is the reason for seeking these additions to the Quebec bench at this particular time.
It is my understanding that the three additional positions for the Ontario County Court really result from the normal increase in litigious business resulting from the growth of the province.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE ADDITIONAL JUDGES FOR ONTARIO AND QUEBEC
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I am glad to see the Minister of Justice here because I wanted to say something very complimentary to him. First of all, I want to congratulate him on his recent appointment of Chief Justice Val Milvain of the trial division of Alberta. I feel he is the type and calibre of man, and I am sure the bar association of Alberta as well as the Canadian Bar Association will agree with me, that we need in this position in Alberta. He will add dignity to the judiciary and will do a fine job as one of the judges of the trial division. I believe, too, he will supply the necessary administrative skill to take care of the backlog that may exist in many of our courts. I should also like to say that we have had very good appointments to the bench. I can speak for the two provinces in which I have practiced, Saskatchewan and Alberta.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE ADDITIONAL JUDGES FOR ONTARIO AND QUEBEC
speechtext: Was he a Tory?

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE ADDITIONAL JUDGES FOR ONTARIO AND QUEBEC
speechtext:
Certainly there have been members of parliament appointed. I have always taken the view that experience gained
October 7, 1968

in parliament is helpful to a judge in coming to a conclusion when certain important cases come before him. On the whole, I would say that appointments to the judiciary have been very good. My friend asked if I want an appointment, but I would tell him that I am quite happy with the position I now hold.
This resolution contains two very simple propositions. As the President of the Privy Council said, on behalf of the Minister of Justice who was absent for a moment, provision is made for increasing the number of County Court judges in Ontario and adding 11 additional judges to the Quebec Superior Court. It goes without saying, and even without mentioning the additional jurisdiction in connection with divorce, that the growth of urban centres in Canada, as in other countries, has increased the work load of the courts of our various provinces. There is a backlog of cases, both civil and criminal. I do not know but perhaps the minister will tell me how many judges of the Quebec Superior Court there are now. In view of the additional jurisdiction in connection with divorce, I would say this resolution results from a recommendation by the Attorney General of Quebec.
When we are talking about the appointment of judges there is one thing I should like to mention to the Minister of Justice. This is no criticism of the present minister. I am referring to cases that come before the superior courts of the provinces in which judgments are reserved. Frequently in this country judgments are reserved for months on end. I know in my own province that at one time some cases had been reserved for two or three years during which time citizens of that province were denied a judgment. The United States system may seem harsh, but after a certain number of cases have piled up on a judge's desk for a certain length of time his salary stops until he catches up. It seems to me these people sometimes procrastinate far too long.
I think it may be well to underline the fact that amendments to the Criminal Code are coming before the house soon. There is not much change, I understand, between the former bill and the new bill in so far as the jurisdiction of the various courts in criminal matters is concerned. There is no doubt that there has been an acceleration in crime, and this was mentioned during the question period. I do not have the statistics before me, but I have a newspaper article with the heading,
Judges Act
"Underworld Toll At 15 In Montreal". The article reads:
The count of "underworld killings" in the Montreal area stood at 14 dead since last February after police discovered the bodies of a young couple in the trunk of a car Saturday.
But by Sunday the toll appeared to have mounted to 15 with the discovery of a young man's body in a car cemetery near Huntingdon, 20 miles southeast of here.
He had been shot and had apparently died of bullet wounds in the head and neck-
[DOT] (5:10 p.m.)
It seems to me that one of the things we must have is a strong police force in order to solve crimes. Then, when criminals are brought before the courts, we need an expedient administration to bring them to trial and, if they are found guilty, to hand out a proper penalty.
There are two kinds of crime, Mr. Chairman. The notion that crime can be described in a single category is erroneous. Violent crime creates a climate of fear in the streets of our growing cities. White collar crime, in economic terms, is much less visible than violent crime. The material cost of crime, such as petty theft, consumer fraud, violations of the Combines Act and embezzlement, dwarfs all crimes of violence, even in Canada. However, to control violent crime and white collar crime, we must have laws that are practical and acceptable to modern and new interpretations of life and human behaviour. One move in the right direction, of course, is to increase the capacity of the courts to handle the cases that come before them.
I might say that I read the recent article in Maclean's magazine, and the minister is a great reporter. I thought that in this regard he was wearing the new jacket of the Prime Minister, whether or not the reforms came from him or from the Prime Minister. However, I recommend to him that he make some real changes in the Criminal Code so as to make our courts expedient. Justice must flow so that everyone has an equal chance, those with money and those without.
Proper laws and proper law enforcement cannot be underestimated in the control of crime, but I have felt for years that we must get at the breeding grounds of crime. Crime breeds in the cesspools of injustice and poverty in the urban slums of our fast growing cities. Urban poverty makes the people who dwell there the victims, not the masters, of their environment. The bad environment becomes the hereditary legacy of the next generation. In order to launch a major assault

October 7. 1968
Judges Act
on crime we must make an attack on the conditions of despair and the denial of human opportunity in which crime can grow. However, crime still thrives under conditions of affluence, and it is the white collar, economic crime which is eroding the capitalistic system and promoting more controls and less freedom.
In brief then, police, courts and prisons cannot alone control crime. We must also deal with the underlying cause of crime-the immense and stubborn forces pervading our environment, measuring our character and determining the quality of our lives.
Through long range effort in a new land of bountiful resources we can conquer poverty, ignorance, disease, discrimination, family breakdown, injustice, social tension and despair. But while we must strive to uproot the causes of crime we must put our practical mind to work to amend the various sections of the Criminal Code to guarantee that the law is respected, that it is not shaped and planned so that it protects the rich and creates injustice against the poor. Crime is a national problem by our constitution, while law enforcement is a provincial and local responsibility. This parliament must direct its processes to ensuring criminal justice. It is for us to bring excellence to every aspect of the administration of criminal justice. That is why I congratulate the Minister of Justice on the calibre of men he has appointed to the bench during his short time in office.
I have dealt with reserved decisions, Mr. Chairman, and I do not quite know what is the answer. Perhaps a letter from the minister to the chief justices of the various provinces would help. We have to cure the problem created by judgments that are reserved for a long time, because this prevents the wheels of justice from turning.
I am also concerned about something I read recently. There is now a bill before the other place, no doubt promoted by the government and which will be here soon, in connection with amending the legislation that deals with the Supreme Court of Canada. We have increased the number of judges of the Superior Court trial division of one province and of the County Court of another, and since this resolution is now before the committee it might be appropriate to consider what will happen under those amendments to the jurisdiction of the Supreme Court of Canada. That bill seeks to put justice on a strictly materialistic basis whereby civil cases will not come before that court, if the bill

becomes law, unless the amount involved is at least $10,000 and unless there is a question of law at stake.
First of all, let me deal with the question of law. I think the Supreme Court of Canada is overworked; there is no question of that. Perhaps the Minister of Justice or the appropriate officials of the crown would consider the possibility of enlarging the court. However, I suggest that before we cut down on the number of cases that come before that court we should be very careful in our approach.
We must remember that if we take away the right of appeal to the Supreme Court of Canada and declare that in civil matters where property or human rights are concerned no one shall come before the court unless the amount involved is at least $10,000 or there is a point of law to be decided, we are shutting the door of justice. People in Canada and also small corporations would be deprived of the right to appeal their cases to the Supreme Court of Canada, the highest court in the land.
The Minister of Justice has been a trial lawyer, like many of us in this house, and he appreciates one of the great responsibilities of a trial judge in the superior court, of whom we shall be shortly naming a number in the province of Quebec. I have often wondered about the kind of power such a judge has but I do not know how to alter this power in our field of jurisprudence. I refer to the power of a trial judge to find the facts of a case.
What do I mean by that? Let me explain it for the benefit of those who do not practise before the bar. For example, ten witnesses on one side of a case may say one thing and one witness on the other side may say another thing about what may be a very simple matter. The trial judge has the power to come to the conclusion that he believes the one witness and to discard the evidence of the ten witnesses. Once he finds this as a fact, Mr. Chairman, you are stuck with that fact in the court of appeal and in the Supreme Court of Canada. This becomes a fact in the case unless you can prove that the judge arrived at a certain set of facts on non-existent evidence. That pretty well puts the formula simply.
When you take away from the Supreme Court of Canada, in spite of the rule of jurisprudence that is a rule of common law and not statute law, the right to be able to review the facts of a case, then I submit that once more you are closing the door of justice. 1 fully realize that there may be a question of
Ociober 7, 1968

mixed law and fact, and whether a trial judge has improperly found a fact based on non-existent evidence may itself be a point of law.
I am against such a step on two grounds. Over the week end Senator Roebuck said- and I agree with him-that we are really shutting the door of justice in the Supreme Court of Canada to citizens of the country if we enact a provision stipulating that cases before that court must involve $10,000 or a question of law. The average citizen of Canada will be denied the right to go before the highest court of the land, which to me is a very dangerous approach to justice.
[DOT] (5:20 p.m.)
In defence of the Supreme Court of Canada may I say that I think its judges are overworked. The judges of that court do not receive the assistance given to judges of the supreme court of the United States, who have many lawyers behind them to help them in research. In this country our judges have no such facilities and that is why they are overworked, no doubt. I say that the answer to that problem is not to cut down the number of cases that come before the Supreme Court but to enlarge the membership of that court, if it needs to be enlarged, just as we are enlarging the membership of the Superior Court of Quebec and the County Courts of Ontario.
Before the Minister of Justice seeks to diminish the jurisdiction of the Supreme Court of Canada he ought to read the speech Senator Roebuck made in the other place last week. He ought to study it well and think about it before taking away the rights of the average people of Canada. I say that even at present our system of justice falls below the level it ought to achieve in any just society. Here I adopt the words of an hon. member to my left who said there is one law for the rich and another law for the poor. That is so. The quality of justice a litigant obtains from the courts all too often is determined by the intelligence and ability of the man who represents him before the bar of justice, whether the action is of a civil or criminal nature. We must be careful before we curtail the jurisdiction of courts.
The President of the Privy Council said that one reason for increasing the number of Quebec judges was that the new divorce law entailed much more work for the courts. It seems to me from what I have learned that the rules and regulations under the new divorce legislation are so cumbersome that
Judges Act
those who seek a remedy under the law meet with two difficulties at the present time. First, since the new procedure is so cumbersome, it has become almost too costly to litigate. I do not know what lawyers are now charging for divorce cases. I have not discussed the matter with members of my firm or with members of the Alberta bar, but I am told that under the new rules lawyers must do a great deal more work than they had to do under the old rules. Therefore citizens must pay a great deal more for a divorce than they paid under the old system.
The second problem also has to do with procedure. Here I refer to an example taken from Ontario. Perhaps the Ontario rules ought to be changed in cases where substitu-t'onal service is required. At present a spouse who has been deserted must publish a notice in a newspaper. However, in order to obtain an order to publish the notice the litigant must swear to an affidavit that his spouse will probably read the newspaper in which the notice is to be published. I ask you, Mr. Chairman, how can anyone swear to such an affidavit, especially if he has not seen his partner for four or five years or if his partner has gone to Timbuktu or somewhere else? That is making an ass of the law, as Charles Dickens would have said.
The Minister of Justice ought to see that the rules, which are far too cumbersome, are changed. The present requirement for the filing of material should also be changed. I do not think that all the material at present required is necessary. Let us streamline the procedure and make it easy for the average citizen to go to court without incurring too great an expense. That way the litigation time will be cut down and the amount of work judges must do will also be reduced.
On the other hand, I have always taken the view that the price we pay for defending the liberty of the subject can never be too great, and that is why I speak on behalf of this resolution. If the provincial governments have made their recommendation then, naturally, I think it ought to be accepted.
