I also think that the
Department of Justice ought to look into the jurisdiction of the Exchequer Court of Canada. First of all, that court leans towards the crown. Whether one brings an action having to do with an expropriation or with any other wrong, that court is a little pro-crown. Second, even under the new rules the procedure of the court is so cumbersome that it is far too costly for the average citizen to litigate in that court.
In my hand I have a newspaper report concerning a case before the Exchequer Court. I should hate to guess how much this matter cost the litigants. The article was printed on October 3, 1968, and is headed, "No Recourse For Japanese, Lawyer Says". I see that an hon. member from British Columbia has looked up. The report reads:
When the government confiscated properties from Japanese-Canadians during the second world war it was forever and without recourse, a federal government lawyer said yesterday.
Norman Mullins-
He is counsel for the Department of Justice.
-was arguing the government's case in a $1,450,000 claim for compensation by Torazo Iwasaki, 89.
Mr. Mullins said the arguments put forward by counsel for Mr. Iwasaki were rejected 21 years ago by a judgment of a similar claim by Eikichi Nakashima.
The article goes on to say that this property was taken from the Japanese owner during the war and that compensation of $5,000 was paid. Mr. Macleod, counsel for Iwasaki, told the Exchequer Court that Gavin C. Mauat-I am not sure how to pronounce that name-an agent of the Secretary of State, was the custodian of enemy property. Now Mauat is one of the leading members of a syndicate that stands to make $1,450,000 out of the property.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE ADDITIONAL JUDGES FOR ONTARIO AND QUEBEC
speechtext:
If my hon. friend wants to make a speech he should do so at the proper time. I do not wish to enter into an argument with a member on the front bench rump.
I should like to see the Minister of Justice examine the jurisdiction of the Exchequer Court of Canada as it relates to property rights of citizens and arrange for matters involving property rights to be taken out of
[The Deputy Chairman.!
the Exchequer Court and placed in the Superior Courts and Supreme Courts of the provinces. In that way litigants could afford to have their cases tried. In that way we could go a long way to remedying the old concept that there is one law for the rich and another for the poor in the Exchequer Court.
At present actions involving expropriations are far too costly for the average citizen. Recently a case involving the green belt had cost the litigant $29,000. He tried to come before the court but could not and gave up the ghost and let the matter go. I say that when we talk about appointing judges to Supreme Courts, Superior Courts, the Queen's Bench division or what have you in the various provinces, our first duty, before enlarging or diminishing any jurisdiction, ought to be to make certain there is not one law for the rich man and another law for the poor man.

There is one other point I should like to make and it has to do with the calibre of judges to be appointed. I refer to a case with which we are all familiar, the case of Whitfield v. Canadian Marconi Company and the decision of the Quebec Court of Appeal, later upheld by the Supreme Court of Canada, with respect to a contract into which the following clause had been written:
Indian and Eskimo villages are considered out of bounds and personnel are prohibited from fraternizing or associating with the native population except in special circumstances. Infringement of these orders is cause for discharge.
One man fraternized with an Eskimo girl. He was fired. He sued his employer for $25,000. The Quebec court in its ruling had this to say:

The court upheld that clause as being a proper one. If ever there was a case of discrimination being applied, this was one. It does seem to me that a case like this emphasizes once again the importance of appointing to our courts men with feeling, vision and a knowledge of humanity, men who understand that the law can never stagnate, can never be regarded as something which is unchangeable. Law, as it is interpreted, must be like a growing tree, growing as circumstances change and as society changes. This is the key to the kind of imagination and influence required of those who are appointed to our courts. For example, the word "banking" meant one thing in 1906, another in 1935 and something entirely different again in 1968. I give this as an example because I recall a case in Alberta which turned on the definition of banking when the Social Credit government came to power and passed some legislation in this field. As I say, the law must be like a growing tree, able to interpret language so as to fit new circumstances, new facets of society. In this way, of course, the courts legislate.

subtopic: SUGGESTED INCREASE OF BASIC OLD AGE PENSION TO $125 PER MONTH

speakeroldname: Mr. Stanley Knowles (Winnipeg North Centre) moved:
speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
subtopic: SUGGESTED INCREASE OF BASIC OLD AGE PENSION TO $125 PER MONTH
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should give immediate consideration to amending the Old Age Security Act to provide for the full amount of the income supplement provided thereunder to be incorporated into the basic pension, for the amount of the basic pension to be increased to $125 per month, for the increase granted each year on account of an increase in the cost of living to reflect the full extent of that increase, and for the eligible age to be lowered immediately to 65, so that all persons in Canada 65 years of age or over who meet the residence requirements will receive a full pension of $125 per month, plus the cost of living increase, without any means test, the full amount of the old age security pension thus being recognized as a matter of right.
He said: Mr. Speaker, there are a great many matters which come before parliament in which I am interested, but this motion relates to the one which has probably had the greatest amount of my attention during the years since I first came here, now nearly 26 years ago. I am reminded that the first time I rose in this House of Commons to speak on the subject of old age pensions I very boldly and courageously urged that the pension be raised from $20 to $25 per month. I had to sit and listen to Mr. Ilsley tell me that this could not be afforded. However, that same Mr. Ilsley before very long did agree to increase that pension to $25 a month, only at that time there was a means test on it and the provinces were required to pay 25 per cent of the pension.
We have come a bit of distance since then, and I now urge that the old age security pension be raised to $125 a month. I also urge that the income test attached to a portion of it, that portion known as the guaranteed income supplement, be wiped out and that the full $125 a month be granted as a pension to all those who meet the age and residence requirements, without any means or income test of any kind. I also suggest that the formula in the legislation for providing a cost of living increase should be altered so that the increase given to our pensioners will reflect the full amount of any increase in the cost of living, not just that portion up to 2 per cent in any one year.
October 7, 1968

As hon. members are aware, I would not stop there so far as the adjusting of pensions is concerned. When one talks about increasing pensions to reflect an increase in the cost of living one is talking about a minimum requirement, namely, that our pensioners should be enabled at least to keep up with the cost of living during their years of retirement. But as I hope I have made clear times without number, I believe we have to go further than this with respect to all our pensions. I think we have to make it possible for people in their years of retirement to enjoy the increased standard of living that our economy makes possible from year to year and from decade to decade. It is not good enough for just the other sections of society, particularly those in their working years, to be in a position to get increases, to share in our increased productivity. That right must also be extended and guaranteed to our retired persons.
Let me come back to the fundamental part of this resolution, which is its request that there be an increase in the amount of the old age pension itself. The statistics that the Department of National Health and Welfare has produced-some of them are to be found by way of answers to questions of mine that have appeared on the order paper-make it clear that our older people definitely need more than the amount of pension they are now getting.
If the guaranteed income supplement, for all its faults, has done anything, it has proven this point. The statistics show that about 60 per cent of our people who receive the old age security pension have been able to qualify for all or part of the guaranteed income supplement. Sixty per cent of that 60 per cent, or a little more in fact-it is about 40 per cent of the total-have been able to qualify for the full amount of the guaranteed income supplement. These statistics illustrate in a very striking way the fact that for most of our people in their retirement years there is little else but their old age security pension. There are people with other sources of income, but those who have enough other income to live as befits life in this day and age are very few.
I say that a society which does not show greater respect and greater regard for its older people is not a just society and does not deserve some of the accolades that are given to it at the present time. I like and enjoy the emphasis on youth in this day and age. I enjoy and support the emphasis being placed
Old Age Security Act
on the proposition that our youth should be given opportunities in education, employment, culture, and all the things that make for a richer and fuller life. I welcome the efforts that are being made, and successfully in many areas, to involve people at younger ages in the processes of democracy, in all of the life of our society. That is good. I support it wholeheartedly. But I submit that our society must not, because of its concern for youth, forget old age. Far too many of our older people in this country are suffering privation, suffering poverty, suffering want in the midst of all the affluence that we have, because we have not provided them with a sufficient pension.
[DOT] (6:10 p.m.)
I recognize that pensions are not the only answer, that we have to do more in the field of housing, in the area of health, and in providing recreational, cultural and other opportunities, including the opportunity to be useful. But to make speeches about these other things that we must do does not take the place of doing this basic, essential thing, namely, increasing the amount of money that we make available to our people. When one looks at the total production in our country today, the money that we are able to find for other things, it just does not make sense that arguments are put up against increasing the amount of the old age pension.
Therefore I urge that this figure of $125 a month be taken very seriously. I urge that the house must not permit the government to try to slough it off, to try to tell us that enough has been done for pensioners and that we must leave the pension where it is. Our old people need the increase, they deserve it, they have the right to it, and we can afford it. If we are going to talk about a just society, these people are entitled to it as much as anyone else.
Now, Mr. Speaker, one of the main elements of this resolution is its point blank call for the abolition of the guranteed income supplement as such, for its incorporation into the basic pension, and for the discontinuance of the idea that a portion of the pension is to be paid on the basis of an income test. I need not remind this house how strenuously I argued against the income or means test, and for the acceptance of the principle of universality and for maintaining that principle in our old age pension legislation. I feel that the return of a portion of the old age pension to an income or means test was a backward step

October 7. 1968
Old Age Security Act
which has done immeasurable harm, and it is a step that we must reverse at the earliest possible time. However, instead of repeating my own arguments, which are to be found on many of the pages of Hansard, I thought I would like to refer again today to an interesting and valuable address that was made in Winnipeg on September 19, 1968, by Dr. Reuben C. Baetz, executive director of the Canadian Welfare Council. Dr. Baetz was addressing the audit workshop of the social service audit at Winnipeg on that date.
What Dr. Baetz had to say is very telling, and I urge the government to pay attention to it. I will read parts of his address. This is what he said:
In our income maintenance programs, especially, we tend unwittingly to disregard the concept of solidarity. In recent months universal income programs, such as flat rate allowances for the aged and family allowances, have been severely criticized. It is argued that we should develop a selective policy in our income maintenance programs, and concentrate our efforts on the poorest sector of the population.
I interrupt to suggest that that is an accurate description of the position being taken by the government today. It is a description of the popular and plausible notion that instead of paying larger pensions to everyone and letting the income tax take care of those who get too much, we should pay pensions on a selective basis. Here is a specialist in the field saying that this idea has to be looked at very closely. Dr. Baetz admits there are arguments on that side, but then he goes on to say:
Nevertheless, a selective policy-
This is the kind that implies an income test so that the pension will be given to those who need it, not to everyone.
*-in income maintenance creates artificially, or at least emphasizes by official flat, an inequality between two social groups, between the one that aids and the one that is aided and is dependent.
Let us pay special attention to the following:
The social segregation which results is, in itself, an affront to the dignity of the whole section of the population.
That is what I said time and time again when the government was bringing in the guaranteed income supplement and putting back an income test-I called it a means test-on a portion of the old age pension. Some people said it is not an insult to have to fill out a form of that kind to get the pension. But here is a specialist in the field saying it

after it has been in effect for a period of time. Dr. Baetz went on to say:
For example, through our stubborn insistence-
That is the government for you.
-at being selective in our income maintenance programs for the aged, we have in fact divided our aged population into two groups-the "haves" and the "have-nots".
Let us listen to this as it describes the tremendous forward step we took back in 1950 when we took the means test off the old age pension. This is what Dr. Baetz said:
For quite a number of years we have provided a flat rate allowance to all regardless of need. The feeling of solidarity among the aged was maintained.
Not only was a feeling of solidarity maintained but one of pride in being retired people and being on the old age pension. It was there. Any of us who lived through the earlier years when the means test was at its worst and then lived through the period when the pension was universal can confirm that the feeling of solidarity among the aged was maintained, and not only solidarity but pride. However, let me quote Dr. Baetz again. He said:
However, two years ago, we introduced a guaranteed income supplement for those aged who can prove their income is low enough to warrant it. One half of the aged population did prove themselves to be eligible for supplementary assistance-
Actually it is 60 per cent.
-through massive paper work. In effect, we have split our aged into two almost evenly divided groups-the "haves" and the "have-nots". Those who need supplementary financial assistance-which is "welfare" in their minds and others-and those who are independent. We have forced thousands of our aged, who struggled all their lives to "stay off relief", to accept this status in their declining years. By increasing the flat rate allowance to $107, and adjusting the income tax rates for higher income groups among the aged, we could have provided the same financial assistance to the aged whose other income was too low, and still maintained the concept of solidarity among the aged.
I could go on quoting other interesting sections from Dr. Baetz' address, but having quoted from it last week I hope hon. members will become interested in it and will get copies of it. I will therefore content myself with just one or two more sentences from his address. He said:
In recent months the concept of universal programs has fallen into disrepute, and selectivity seems now to be the ascendant theme.
How true that is. People are saying, "let us use the money to give it to those who need
October 7, 1988

it". This sounds plausible, and very compassionate, but Dr. Baetz says:
I would hope that before we throw out our universal programs we should more thoroughly examine their weaknesses and strengths, one of which is the maintenance of the feeling of solidarity among all Canadians.
I come back again to the theme on which I have rung the changes so often. I have been interested in the subject of old age pensions and in old age pensioners long enough to have seen three distinct periods in its administration. First, there was the period when the first old age pension with its means test was in effect, when it was a disgrace to be on it and when people had to submit to the indignity of a vicious means test to get it. It was a period to which we do not want to go back at all. Second, there was the period from about 1951 to 1966 or so when the old age pension of various amounts, $40, $46, $55, $65 or $75 a month, was universal and everyone who was at the right age received it. At that time it became a matter of pride to be a pensioner. Now we are in a period when we have divided our old age people into two groups: Those who get the pension and have enough so that they do not get the supplement, and those whose condition is such that they have to go through the test, and their pride of being on the pension is already diminishing.
My arguments are well known, but I hope it makes some impression on this house that I am relying so heavily today on a specialist in the field, Dr. Reuben Baetz, executive director of the Canadian Welfare Council. He says very briefly what we in this corner said when this matter was under debate. We could have achieved the same purpose, we could have got the money through to the people who needed it, by making a universal payment, doing away with all this massive paper work that was unnecessary, but leaving it to the income tax to take back from those-and they are few-who do not need any surplus that it was inappropriate for them to receive.
I hope that we have not gone too far down this road of selectivity and too far away from the principle of universality. It is still in my view one of the finest moments in the history of this parliament when we took the means test off in 1950 or 1951, and I still think the way to establish not only an adequate level of income for our senior citizens but to give them pride in being part of that way of life which is old age is by giving the full old age pension as a matter of right.
Old Age Security Act

I hope, Mr. Speaker, we will not be faced with the argument that because the means test supplement was enacted only a couple of years ago we must stick with it. It is with pleasure, Mr. Speaker, that I take advantage of this opportunity to address myself to the house in respect of the question raised by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles). I sympathize, like everyone in this house, with the problems of our senior citizens. I can say honestly that I share with the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre his concern for these people. We would like them to have sufficient income to enable them to live with integrity, to live on a proper standard, during those later years of their lives.
The points the hon. member made in the resolution are simple. The first is that this problem deserves immediate attention. I think that is true. I think that the whole problem of social security in this country deserves immediate attention. In addition, the problem of unemployment deserves immediate attention. I could stand here for 20

October 7, 1988
Old Age Security Act
minutes and sound oft about all the things with which we have to deal that deserve immediate attention. It is a matter of priority. I, for one, do not feel competent to say where this particular subject should be placed in the order of priorities.
I believe it is true that there are many people-I know there are in my riding

who are older and who suffer from the problems of inflation. They have fixed incomes and have great difficulty in establishing a satisfactory standard of living. This does not mean, however, that I feel the real solution would be to give them an income of $125 a month, which is not much more than they are getting at present. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre seemed to think that we should do away with the guaranteed income supplement and incorporate it into the old age security pension. This statement is a surprise to me because I would have thought the members of the New Democratic party would have welcomed some approach toward achieving a guaranteed income. I would have thought the principle of the guaranteed income supplement would have been more important than the other principle. However, it seems they want to do away with the income supplement itself. Perhaps in the guaranteed income we would find a solution to the whole social problem.
We have a mass of social welfare programs. I believe they cost this government well over $1 billion a year. Perhaps the real solution is to marry all these social programs into a master program. Perhaps it could take the form of a guaranteed income supplement so that we could look after the needs of all the people of this country who really try to look after themselves but, because of the position in which they find themselves, are not capable of doing so. The proposal to increase the income to $125 a month and to tie it to the increase in the cost of living is not really much different from what we have now. Mind you, the difference is important to those people in that age category. At the present moment, and I believe I am correct, the payment per month to these people is over $107.
I admit this is less than $125, but with the escalator clause and the way things are going we will soon achieve that level.
Another point the hon. member made was that we should lower the eligible age to 65. At the moment the eligible age is 67. In 1969 it will drop to 66 and in 1970 it will drop to 65.
I do not see, therefore, that there is that much difference at the moment. So far as the means
[Mr. Cafik.l
test is concerned, to which the hon. member referred, I would agree with him it should be eliminated if it were a means test. I do not think it is. It is one thing to say we are going to give a benefit to those who have an income of less than a certain figure, but it is something else again to make people sell their homes and find out how much money they have in the bank before they can qualify for a pension. I may be wrong, but I believe the only qualification is that people cannot earn more than a certain amount. I believe the government will supplement incomes to enable people to earn up to $1,260 each year. This is quite a different thing from a means test. I, for one, do not really think it is embarrassing. I think the whole problem of social security, or part of it at least, is to make sure we help those who are genuinely in need. I think everyone would agree with that.
I believe we must find an approach to this problem and to all social security problems that will eliminate to some extent aid which is given to those who do not need it. We should have a master program so that we can eliminate many of the abuses that exist in our social assistance and welfare programs. While this may not be apropos to the question of old age pensions and old age security, I think it is important that whatever welfare programs we implement we recognize that we must never create an atmosphere in which people believe the world owes them a living, that there is no point in saving or that there is no point in trying to provide for yourself because the government will look after you. We want to look after those who are in need. I feel we have a distinct obligation to pay great respect and show great concern for the interests of our elderly people. I, for one, will take no back seat in that connection to anyone in this house. I believe all of us share that concern.
I believe there is a need here. I know that many people within the existing programs need help. I will do anything I can to support any measure to help them. I know that I need more information on the subject before I can make a basic decision. I suggest that this problem should be considered by a parliamentary committee, and considered most carefully. In this way we would make sure that whatever we decide will be in the best interests of both our country and our senior citizens.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to say a few words on this notice of motion that has been moved by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles). It is really in four parts, the first of which suggests that the house should give immediate consideration to amending the Old Age Security Act to provide for the full amount of the income supplement provided thereunder to be incorporated into the basic pension.
I am convinced, Mr. Speaker, that the present guaranteed income supplement has had the effect that I said it would have when it first came into being, and that is to cause an awful lot of hardship and headache to many recipients. I made the prediction, Mr. Speaker, that if we went back to a means test- which is really what it is-many elderly people, not because of any ill intent or that sort of thing, but purely inadvertently, would report their income wrongly. I am sure the huge majority of our elderly citizens were convinced that they had reported their incomes correctly; but correct or not, I know of literally dozens of instances in my constituency-and I am sure this number is multiplied 264 times across Canada-who applied for additional assistance under the guaranteed income supplement, made an error in their application, and subsequently had their cheques reduced because the government felt obliged to recover the overpayment.
As I said, Mr. Speaker, this has caused tremendous hardship to many people. I have seen many cases where not only the guaranteed income supplement which had been paid in error was cut off, but where the basic pension cheque during this year, 1968, was cut below $76.50 which, due to the increase in the cost of living, about which I shall say a word or two presently, is now the basic amount of the pension. I predicted that going back to a means test would not mean that everything would run smoothly. I claimed, as did others, that hardship would be caused to many people.
As minister of the Department of National Health and Welfare for almost six years, I had experience in the fact that, under the old age assistance scheme people between 65 and 70 could claim assistance after meeting a means test. They would then find out subsequently that they had made an error in reporting their income-again inadvertently. However, according to the law the government had to claim a portion of their old age security
Old Age Security Act
cheque after they became eligible for old age security at 70 years of age. I have known cases, Mr. Speaker, where people in receipt of old age security and the guaranteed income supplement have had for several months to suffer a cut to less than $76.50 a month, and this has caused untold hardship.
Another thing that bothers me is this. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre quoted Dr. Reuben Baetz and referred to the affront to dignity that is faced by people who have applied for the guaranteed income supplement. I feel that this affront is wrong, Mr. Speaker.
I should like to remind the house of the report of a committee made in 1950. This was a joint committee of the House of Commons and Senate and was composed of members from all parties of this house. Although I did not enter the house until two or three years after that report, if I am not mistaken the committee's report was unanimous. This was the first time there had been a unanimous report of a joint committee of this house and the other place, Mr. Speaker. This committee had studied the problem for months and months, and had finally arrived at a plan to give people a basic old age pension without a means test, which it felt was the correct thing to do. I feel that it is still the right decision to make today. It is all very well to say that we want to help those who need it most; I agree with that. But at the same time, Mr. Speaker, people are suffering today as a result of the present system of paying the guaranteed income supplement.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to take a few minutes to speak on this resolution, and to congratulate the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles! for having brought the question before the house, as I think it is very important.
First, I think that this notice of motion contains four main ideas, one of which is to increase the present pensions about which, Mr. Speaker, I will say only a few words. I think that, in view of the present cost of living, pensions could easily be increased, especially when an old person lives alone. When two people live together, even with the present pension, they can manage up to a certain point, because they have some common expenses, for example rent or housing, electricity and certain other related expenses.
However, an old person living alone finds it difficult to live adequately on the pension he now gets. I therefore feel that the house should study the possibility of increasing that pension to enable those who get only that pension to live more comfortably, more adequately and to feel less closely watched, especially by government inspectors whom some of them call hunting dogs.
At this stage, Mr. Speaker, I come precisely to that part of the speech by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre where he asked that the guaranteed income supplement be granted without any means test. I fully agree with the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre on that point, as well as some of my colleagues in the Ralliement Creditiste and other hon. members I will not mention and who spoke at length on that matter.
When this amendment to the Old Age Security Act came before the house, we had anticipated the difficulties which the income test would mean for the aged people claiming the $30 supplement who would have to give an account of their income.
Mr. Speaker, last Saturday-hardly two days ago-an old lady on the verge of bursting into tears came to my office, saying that the Department of National Health and Welfare was demanding the return of an overpayment out of the $76.50 pension now being

paid to her. What happened in her case? Since her husband's death, that lady had had federal, provincial and even municipal officials looking through all her papers and her bank accounts to see whether she had some income hidden somewhere. Fed up with having strangers know more about her personal affairs than she did herself, she had refused to reveal to the government what little capital she had in reserve precisely to meet possible difficulties. On those grounds, legal claim was made to the amount which it seems she had been paid and to which she was not entitled, and that without knowing exactly what her financial situation was.
This is one of the many cases of which the members are aware, I believe, concerning the old people who feel persecuted through those investigations. I therefore fully agree that the system of checking should be abolished as soon as possible, and I doubt that sending the resolution to a committee for study would improve the situation, because more protracted debates would keep the government from acting, thus delaying the setting up of a just society.
So, I feel that the government should take it upon itself to make the necessary amendments now, during the current session, to improve the act and grant immediately, and without tests, all old persons 65 years of age-as a spokesman of the government said a while ago, without waiting for the present provisions of the act to take effect-a $109 pension from the beginning of next January; or to increase the pension to $125 as proposed by the mover. Indeed, the government need not refer this resolution to a house committee; it can do so on its own.

Mr. Speaker, at this point, I merely wish to add a few words which, I trust, my colleagues can easily remember.
First of all, I congratulate my good friend for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) for having proved, once again, as always, that he is an inveterate defender of those classes of society which certainly need help.
I should also like to congratulate those who have spoken in this regard, for I feel that this is more than a question of dollars. Although we, in this corner of the house, at times feel that we need field glasses to see your elegance in the chair, Mr. Speaker, nonetheless we are members of this house and we want to express our opinions as much as possible. I trust that note will be taken of this. I say this is not merely a question of dollars, and I feel
October 7, 1968

that if we grant everyone $125 this year, next year it will be $135, $140 or $150.
In my opinion, the most disadvantaged segment of our population is that which is over 65. Why? Because it is a problem which those who are 30, 40 or 50 have never thought about and have never tried to solve. The answer is simple. Today, under our present economic system, people retire at 65. Some like to be called pensioners and others do not. Anyway, whether they like it or not, they are pensioners. These people find it difficult to make ends meet and often die soon after they retire. I think that we should give greater consideration to the problem of ageing.
My hon. friend mentioned earlier Professor Baetz. I might suggest that he read an article written by Dr. Bortz entitled Our Ageing Population. That, I think, is the whole problem: gerontology.
As an example, there is no amount appropriated for gerontology in the estimates of the National Research Council of Canada. In 1960, people over 65 years made up 8.6 per cent of the population of Canada and 10 years from now the proportion will be 10 to 12 per cent. What are we going to do with the aged? Shall we give them $140, $150? In my view, it is not only a question of rehabilitating them but an economic question as well.
Medicine is making constant progress, whether we like it or not. The estimated span of life nowadays is 72 years. Within 10 years, perhaps it will reach 76 or 77 years. People will enjoy a green old age and perfect health. Old people will be in a certain way useless to society. I believe we are making a mistake. That is the reason why I said a moment ago that this is the problem of the people who are 30, 40 and 50, and they are the ones who should endeavour to set up a scheme of occupational therapy. This is called ergotherapy in medical terms. It is a kind of therapy which makes it possible for those people to enjoy the economic advantages available instead of suffering the disadvantages which seem to be their lot.
[DOT] (6:50 p.m.)
If we remove these people from the labour market at the age of 65, if their number increases in 10 or 12 years, as I said earlier, our productivity will certainly decrease. Now, if our productivity decreases, another group of people will have to work more to balance it out. These people raise problems in the field of housing, for instance.
Old Age Security Act
Earlier I heard my very good friend talk about an old lady who came to his office. He is very lucky to have seen only one; I have seen them by the hundreds. Every day for instance, I see people who need drugs. They do not have the means to obtain them and even if they received $125 or $150 a month, they would be poorer than if they could be covered by a drug insurance. If these people could be assisted in other fields, besides money, it would be a lot better in my opinion.
We were talking a while ago of statistics; I have here figures that are quite surprising. In the United States, for instance, it is said that the population will show an increase of 20 per cent in the next decade, while the number of workers will increase only by 6 per cent. Twenty years from now, if those figures are correct, and as they can be ascertained in the book entitled America Next Twenty Years, the population will increase by 40 per cent, but the increase in the number of workers will be only 10 per cent. This means that a worker will not only be self-supporting but able to provide for one person and a half, with all that is coming as concerns labour reform, etc.-

They will have to support themselves and three and a half other persons. In other words, to maintain today's standard of living tomorrow's worker will have to more than double his activity.

Then people having reached the age of 65 can perform certain functions, that is true. According to statistics, five out of eight persons over 65 can accomplish a great deal of work, and interesting work too. And this will not penalize those less than 65 years old, because after all, it is a penalty. It is a penalty because as people over 65 cannot work, people less than 65 have to pay a tax. In the mean time, this deprives the taxation department of some revenues that could be obtained by levying a tax on people over 65 who earn something.
This means, therefore, that we are living in a rapidly changing society, in a society that seems to seek itself. In short we live in a sick society and it is up to us to legislate, not in a unilateral sense, but in a sense that could bring something practical to this society which is changing too rapidly, I would say.
It is up to us to give funds, to induce researchers, especially in geriatrics, to find solutions to the serious problem of ageing. Nowadays, university people are trying to

find vaccines, everything is being done to extend the limits of life. But once a person is 65 years old, we abandon him. He is alone in life. I think those people are the most destitute, the most unfortunate. They still feel able to do something and we are not enabling them to do anything that would permit them to become more or less an asset to society. I think that we still need experienced people today, people who have been through economic hardships like the older members of this house knew in 1933. I feel that it rests with the Canadian people to wake up and to be sensitized to that important problem; it is a problem of the survival for a nation.
Do we realize that, with the pill, one day we will have to cope with the fall in the birth-rate? We speak about genocide in Bia-fra and many other things. The real genocide is committed by the white man and will eventually experience the consequences. We do not have to worry about it, Mr. Speaker. When we are still dashingly young we do not think about tomorrow or illness, we do not think that one day we will be 65 years of age and that we will be retired from the Canadian economic life.
Now, I would like this matter to be taken into serious consideration and every effort made so that the people will understand that the real problem is not that of a $125 pension.
I greatly admire those who have served the country, whether it be in the public service or in the armed forces, in the defence of our rights on foreign battlefields during the last three wars. I have great confidence in these people, and if it were possible for me to do so, I would give them everything, because they deserve it. I think the fact of giving something is only a poultice on a wound; it is not a treatment.
I believe that today we should not work out compromise policies but rather planning policies that would at last bring about a sound economic system that would likely benefit the young people who are 65 years of age, because at that age, we can still be young, Mr. Speaker.
There are some people who are still active at 80. As a matter of fact, Professor Dudley White, the great American cardiologist, celebrated his 80th birthday last year. I think we need people who have lived that long, because their lives have been interesting. They knew how to use their heads and their hands to do something and eliminate the fatal boredom of those who no longer feel useful past the age of 65. All soldiers, young and

old, are needed by society, particularly experienced people such as those and people who only ask for an opportunity to do something useful for a society that appears to be very sick.

Mr. Speaker, just before the private members hour I was saying it is a well known fact that the Farm Improvement Loans Act is administered by the banks. Some time ago the banks informed the finance committee of this house that they aimed to lend out about 30 per cent of their money in what are generally conceived to be small loans. I am really more than a bit disappointed that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson), who is now back in Canada, has not taken a greater interest in this debate because the manner in which banks operate and their service to Canadians come under his jurisdiction. I recognize that if the minister had incorporated a fixed interest rate in this bill the banks might not lend any money at all under its terms. I ask how far the banks are prepared to go to serve the Canadian people and the various segments of Canadian industry? A number of years ago when the whole question of banking was being thoroughly studied by the finance committee we were informed that western Canada is a bank depository surplus area, and that it provides a depository surplus from which banks can lend money.
At the resolution stage of this bill the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Olson) stated that the banks became hesitant to lend money at 5 per cent under this legislation, even before the act ran out on June 30 of last year. We are not in any way saying that they have to lend all their money at 5 per cent. I would not suggest that they should not make a profit on lending money, but I do say that in giving a bank a charter we stipulate that it has to provide a service to the community. This is a licence which banks should dearly cherish. They should be prepared to help out various segments of the economy if help is required, and especially so under the terms of this legislation, which provide a government guarantee.
DEBATES	893
Farm Improvement Loans Act
I have taken a rough look at this bill, and after doing so I wonder what the Minister of Finance has in mind. Is he trying to assist small banking companies? Is he trying to assist trust companies and loan companies? When he was speaking on the hustings the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) said his government would set up a separate policy for small farmers, giving them more aid than is available to farmers who are already on economic units. But this bill suggests that the government is giving aid to small banks and near banks, the latter being a term that was applied to such companies some years ago. This bill is an attempt to benefit the near banks and bring them under the government guarantee, something they had not enjoyed previously. There is really no heart shown for the agriculture industry in this legislation.
The minister said that the act came into being in 1945, and I am the first to agree with him that it has served a great purpose since that time. From July to September of last year something like $55 million was lent by the banks under the terms of the Farm Improvement Loans Act. There was a government guarantee at that time. I would like to know how much money the banks lent for farm machinery in the same period this year, without a guarantee?
I know the banks are telling the Minister of Finance that this government guarantee is not necessary any more, that the agricultural industry is a reliable one, and that this guarantee is not really worth a 1 per cent interest rate. They are telling the minister that they have to charge farmers a high rate of interest. If that be the case, then why are machinery sales during the first seven months of this year down 30 per cent in Saskatchewan, 26 per cent in Alberta and 22.8 per cent in Manitoba? That is a drastic reduction. It is interesting to link that with the fact that the farm improvement loans legislation was not in effect for a three or four month period.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I recall that the other day when we were discussing this legislation in resolution form it was suggested that there was an urgency here; that it was important that this legislation go through quickly because the farmers were waiting and needed the credit that would be available under the legislation. They needed this credit program working again, because for all practical purposes it has not been working for almost a year.
This piece of legislation is the one that is supposed to be most urgent. If this is so, I really do not quite comprehend why such extensive changes are being made to the act

at this time. I would have thought that if it was considered urgent-and I would have to agree that it is-it would have been advisable to take the act as it was, put it before this house, and then take a later opportunity to put some of the suggested changes before a standing committee so they could be carefully considered.
I believe that at least one or two fairly important departures have been made in this bill. One is the inclusion of land as an added security or as an added purpose for which money can be lent. This will be the first time land has been included in the act, which as the previous speaker said came into force in 1944 or 1945. The manner in which this provision and the proposals with respect to it are included is, it seems to me, a departure from what has come to be, shall I say the established approach to farm credit in this country. Indeed this does not apply to Canada only but to the United States, our neighbour to the south, and Europe. In effect, comparatively speaking this is short term credit for the purpose of buying land, or perhaps more properly I should say it is intermediate term credit.
In the immediate post second world war period our farmers were starved of credit. They were short of credit; they could not get it because the banks and the standard lending institutions would not make it available at that time, for understandable reasons, one being that they had taken a pretty good shellacking in the 1930's. I can recall the farm organizations, the farm unions and the Canadian Federation of Agriculture saying that a credit program was needed for farmers.
One of the principles put forward by these organizations and the economists was that long term credit was needed for the purchase of land because short term credit is a risky method of putting up money for such a purchase. All the economists that I know seemed to agree with this principle. So the program was started with a 20 year term for repaying the loan. That term was increased to 25 years, then 30 years, and in the last two or three years economists have been talking about perpetual mortgages on farms.
The idea has been that money would be lent and there would be no real intention of repaying it; that it would simply be a charge against the productivity of the land and transferred from one generation to another. I do not know that I agree with this idea, but it is a trend in the thinking.
October 7, 1968	COMMONS
[DOT] (8:30 p.ra.)
One of the economists at the University of Manitoba gave a talk on this subject a year ago. Now, under this legislation, we are regressing when we say we will go back to the granting of intermediate credit on land. We expect that the purchaser will pay this off in 15 years, which is contrary to our previous policy. Now we know that under the present circumstances farmers are not able to build up their own capital. I think it was Mr. John Dawson, who was with the Economic Council of Canada, who said that there was only a short period in the late 1940s and early 1950s during which farmers were able to make enough income from their farms to build up sufficient capital to replace their machinery and to expand and develop their farms, taking advantage of the new technology. The same report from the Economic Council of Canada stated that from time to time we had been depending on credit, and according to most predictions we will continue to do so with the greater use of the new technology.
However, the legislation before us proposes quite the opposite and, in fact, goes against this trend. It may be that some new wisdom has descended on the Department of Agriculture, which has come to the conclusion that this trend is no longer the right one and that we had better consider a new way. This seems to be the sort of approach which is now acceptable, to start a new trend. Perhaps the legislation before us reflects the new trend. For example, within our credit programs we have developed a new approach whereby credit supervisors in the Farm Credit Corporation are able to say to a farmer, "if you want this loan of several thousand dollars, we will sit down with you and see how you can use this money, and how it can be tailored to your operation". Under the farm improvement loan proposals in this bill we will leave it to an insurance company, a trust company or to a bank, whoever may be making the loan, to decide to whom to grant the loan, wherever they think the security is sound, and that we will then underwrite it. If it turns out badly we will pick up the pieces.
I do not consider this to be a really new advance.
It was only a year or two ago that in the maritimes the Farm Credit Corporation decided not to collect payments for a year. I suppose this was helpful to the farmers there and I hope that since then their situation has improved. What will happen if the same situation should arise again in other parts of

The matter of the interest rate was already discussed here by the previous speaker. I am not sure that I can add a great deal, except to state the obvious, namely that we know that there is a limited earning capacity in farming and the only thing that we can do to help is to keep down the interest rate. Such are the circumstances now that farmers are being hemmed in on all sides. With respect to grain, we are limited by the GATT agreement, and the international situation is tough on farmers.
A few days ago we had here in Ottawa the group of corn growers who have requested us to block purchases from the United States. This is a pretty difficult problem. The government proposes to put trust companies, insurance companies and banks back in the lending field, with government guarantees, although these institutions have had considerable difficulties in this respect. This is not necessarily a reflection on the institutions but rather a reflection on the facts of life. Farm Improvement Loans Act with the rate of interest to be charged. This is the crux of the matter, the purpose of the bill.
Although other supporting amendments maybe generally acceptable for various reasons, I think the main question which comes to us as members of the opposition is what criteria the minister will use in determining the interest rates, and on what basis the farmers will have to decide from day to day whether it would be in their interest to hold off borrowing money or whether it would be in the interest of the machine dealers to try to stall a sale for a month or so, thereby giving the farmers the best advantage.

I am concerned because I thought the Liberal party advocated a specific policy for the small farmer. I quote from this statement:
While the situation varies from commodity to commodity, in general 30 per cent of Canada's farmers produce 70 per cent of our agricultural production. This great variation in farm size, and with it productivity, renders the development of agricultural programs appropriate to varying farm sizes most difficult. The problem could be met through the institution of a system of farm differentiation by productivity and size. This differentiation could provide a basis for modifying programs to meet the particular needs of farms of different sizes. The concept is that farmers themselves could reach the decision as to their own classification for this purpose. All farm programs could then be designed taking into consideration the special needs of the smaller farmers and the social aspect of such programs could be recognized and measured. Programs for all other farms could be those

consistent with a larger scale viable operation. In return for the differential level of assistance the smaller farmer could undertake that at the time the farm passed from his possession he would not dispose of it for other than farm consolidation or for movement into the public sector. Thus the special programs designed for farmers in this category would not perpetuate the problem.
The farm improvement loan provision would be extended and integrated with the Farm Credit Corporation. So far as I can see, the only integration is going to be a higher rate of interest. -the long run results would be the elimination of small, uneconomic units and the large subsidies paid to them.

Will this policy apply all across the board? What will happen if we have a situation such as we have this year, one wherein, when harvest time arrives, we have not taken off the crop? interest rate prevent us from going to the bank? What are we to expect? Can the minister give us some idea? Can he tie his formula to anything so that we will not be guessing from day to day?

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to add my voice in the debate by making a few comments in our discussion of Bill No. C-lll to amend the Farm Improvement Loans Act. It is now almost a year since the benefit of the farm improvement loan legislation has gone awry and farmers across Canada have

been labouring with the problem of trying to get adequate farm credit. As was pointed out earlier this evening, the Economic Council, in analysing the economic situation of the agricultural industry of this country, has indicated in no uncertain terms that one problem that is facing the industry is the lack of proper and reasonable credit.
As has been mentioned before, Mr. Speaker, and should be emphasized again, the agricultural industry is the second largest source of income for Canada. The wood, pulp and paper industry is, I think, the major source of income for Canada; but agricultural products take second place. I think hon. gentlemen opposite, Mr. Speaker, have realized a number of times since they took office in 1963 that it is only because of the ingenuity, the perseverance, the tenacity, the technological advance and good economic judgment of the farming industry that we have been able to bail ourselves out of a serious position, so far as the balance of trade problem is concerned.
In 1968, Mr. Speaker, we find the agricultural industry in a very serious financial position, not only because of the effect of inclement weather, frost and so on on this year's crop, but because of the lapse of the world international wheat agreement, which has caused the greatest pile-up of wheat in Canada's history.
Today our farmers owe many bills. They are staggering under the increase in overheads and the cost-price squeeze. It looks as if by design the government is trying to aggravate the situation by bringing in this bill. We are almost in the position of having to buy a pig in a poke.
I do not think this is fair to the agricultural industry, Mr. Speaker. It should have the same consideration as any other. I am greatly discouraged by some of the arguments advanced. I am sure hon. members on this side of the house from western agricultural areas, as well as those who sit opposite, representing agricultural areas, are distressed to hear it asked why the farmers should get a subsidy, why they should not fend for themselves the same as others.
I should like to remind you, Mr. Speaker, and through you the members of the house, that the farming industry is in a very unique position compared with other sectors of the economy. The farmers of this country have no basic control over their economic prospects. On the other hand, if labourers in Canada are dissatisfied with their income, then under the law they can go on strike and demand higher wages in order to obtain their share of the
October 7, 1968

economy. Industry and business are the same. When I, in common with other small businessmen, find myself facing economic problems brought on by rising costs, I raise my prices in order to obtain a fair mark-up and to stay in business. It is the same with the wholesalers, and it is the same in practically every industry across this country. But the farmers are in a unique position. They must rely on mother nature. The farmer cannot go out in the spring and say, "I will leave my tractor in the shed and let it rust, because the cows will calf, the chickens will lay eggs and the pigs will farrow." speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Bill No. C-lll is, naturally, a continuation of the resolutions we were considering the other day, when I mentioned the importance of the agricultural sector in our Canadian economy. I also maintained, among other things, that agriculture is the very basis of the economic structure of Canada. I am still of that opinion. It is one which we express everywhere in Canada and particularly in the east, without, however, discriminating on that account against other parts of the country.
For example, in order to help the western farmers, we accepted and supported legislation likely to help them, and we believe that hon. members from the west will likewise support us in our demands in the eastern part of the country, that is, a uniform agricultural policy for both eastern and western Canada.
In the past, we have noted that there were economic disparities. Now, we also have agricultural disparities. Western farmers are treated better than eastern farmers. Having to deal with many kinds of products, eastern farmers were unable to sell their products or get subsidies, when such subsidies were granted, for example, for wheat production and even for non-production of wheat.

A few days ago, I received letters from Canadians in western Canada informing me that the wheat crop was left to rot this year, because the crop insurance was more beneficial to the western farmer than the subsidies paid by the government. This means that wheat will rot under the snow this winter, since crop insurance is more profitable than government subsidies. Now, while production is being destroyed this way, the honourable Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Olson) is introducing bills allowing farmers to get deeper into debt, to enlarge their farm by enabling them to borrow $25,000 instead of $15,000.

Only, that same Minister of Agriculture was once an active member of the Canadian Social Credit and, at that time, he violently denounced similar bills, sometimes accusing the Conservative government, sometimes the Liberal government, of wanting to crush or stifle the Canadian farmer. Mr. Speaker, it is inconceivable, even incomprehensible, that a man should suddenly change his political allegiance and propose to us today what he fought yesterday, worship today what he fought yesterday.
Mr. Speaker, we are now studying bills Nos. C-110, C-lll and C-112. Those three bills, instead of helping the farmers, place them in a difficult position. A farmer will feel quite free because he will be able to borrow $25,000 to buy machinery and more land to increase the acreage he is farming at the present time. However, when the time comes to pay back capital and interests, he will find himself in a situation even more difficult than at present. The Minister of Agriculture should anticipate that. Anyhow, he knows that when the time comes for repayment, it is painful. We noticed that not only in the field of agriculture but also in every field of economic activity in Canada. Everything goes well when a loan is granted. When the time comes for repayment plus the interests, some suffer headaches. Farmers have been in that state of stagnation for many years.
In 1946, when I came to this house-22 years ago-farmers were facing exactly the same problem as today.
It was difficult for the farmer to sell his production and he could hardly borrow, either under national or provincial farm loans. At least, I know that there was a farm credit board in the province of Quebec. Now, it is a Farm Credit Corporation that governs us at this time. The government undertakes to guarantee the loans and borrowings of farmers up to $25,000, but it does not have the courage to tell them: You will not have to pay an interest rate higher than the one that has been set. Farmers are left an open prey to all the exploiters that will want to lend them money, in order that they may purchase farm lands. As a matter of fact, these lands will cost in 15 years twice as much as their original purchase price. Even if the interest rate


were increased to 8, 9 or 10 per cent, the Minister of Agriculture could at the same time include in this Bill No. C-lll, a subsection in which it would be stipulated that the government undertakes to pay a subsidy equal to 2, 3 or 4 per cent, so that the farmers would be assured of paying nothing more than 2 or 3 per cent interest. Then the minister would help the farmers. For the time being, with that bill the minister is convinced that he is not helping the farmer and that the finance companies will benefit from this bill. Even if one believes, at a given time, that the farmer will benefit therefrom, in the long run, it will be the financiers, those who will lend money to the farmer, who will draw the greatest advantages and, as in the past, the farmers will have to face the same problems.
As I said before, the problem does not boil down to having the farmer produce. He could produce five times more than he does now if he could only be sure of selling his production at prices which would allow him to make profits. The minister knew that when he received the delegation of the Canadian corn producers. The other day, he was told on parliament hill that these people were operating at a loss. Even though they would treble their land, their loss would only be trebled.
In the field of the dairy industry, the same problem is the same. In the field of wheat production, it is the same thing.
We are now selling our wheat to the Russians at a price lower than the costs incurred for its production in western Canada. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Olson) is aware of that. Even if western farmers were allowed to borrow $25,000 to triple the area of their farm in order to produce more wheat, if we are going to sell it at a loss, what advantage will farmers draw therefrom? Will it be profitable? We have absolutely no assurance. Such bills will not improve the standing of agriculture or assure the economic stability of farmers. Those means should not be used.
If the minister brought in a bill, for example, providing for the construction of cold storage plants throughout Canada, that would not only enable us to meet the needs of the Canadian people by storing commodities but it would also enable us to help the emergent countries of the world. Then, the farmer would be sure to sell his products at a profit and the hon. Minister of Agriculture would have saved agriculture and Canadian farmers.
What we need is action and we should stop beating around the bush. Let us not introduce

any more legislation which looks for difficulties where there are none, but instead let us try to bring a solution to the problems. As I said, a farmer who borrows $10,000, $15,000, $20,000 or $25,000 may feel that he is getting substantial help, but 10 years from now, Mr. Speaker, if we are still in this house, the farmers will experience far more serious problems than they have to face now. So, I say frankly that these bills are not meant to assist the farmer; on the contrary, they tend to mortgage his farm a little more and to enslave him, and this is the fault of the present government and the one we had before.
Mr. Speaker, the farmers deserve attention from the minister, from the government and from parliament, and although we do not all come from agricultural constituencies, it is nonetheless true that agriculture is the basis of the whole national economy. As a matter of fact, L. B. Johnson, who is now president, said not so long ago, that returning to the land could be the solution to the depression now looming up in the United States.
It is the same with us. Thirty years ago, we witnessed a back-to-the-farm movement. It was said that leaving the cities to settle on farms would solve the problem of poverty amidst affluence. We practised colonization on a very large scale, and, at that time, in the northwestern part of Quebec, in the Quebec and the Lac-Saint-Jean area, in the Saguenay and even in northern Alberta and Saskatchewan, most of the parishes were founded. It was back to the land. Well, today, with the problems which crop up in the cities, I am convinced that instead of saying: Let us cut down the number of farms, the minister will have to say, as in the past: The back-to-the-farm movement might be the ideal solution to the depression in order to face the misery which is anticipated in the cities this coming winter, not within 10 years but this winter, because we will have to face an increasing number of unemployed, not because people do not have the opportunity to purchase commodities, but simply because they cannot afford them. At the present time, the farmers cannot afford to buy land or incur expenses to increase their production because they have no assurance that they will sell their surplus production, they are not even sure of selling this year's production.

Is he, perhaps, trying to put down a revolt? Is he having second thoughts? Did he receive a message from the prophetic Bible Institute of Calgary? Or is this a manoeuvre setting the stage so as to justify the change of interest rate proposed in connection with the farm credit legislation?
This bill does three main things. It changes the manner in which interest rates are set. Under the new arrangements the governor in council will have the power to set interest rates, whereas formerly the rate was fixed at 5 per cent. In the second place it extends farm improvement loan coverage to include

The argument has been made that the level of returns in agriculture at the present time is insufficient to carry high interest rates. It has been noted in this house that this report was used as the basis for the Farm Credit Act as it was originally introduced in this house. I should like to draw the minister's attention to some of the principles that were set out by this royal commission for a public credit program. It did suggest that a farm should be treated as a unit for credit purposes. Second, it suggests that credit is needed by the young farmer with practical experience but a shortage of capital. Third, it suggests there is a greater need for credit facilities and, fourth, there is a need for an assessment of applications for credit and the income potential of the potential borrower. What we do need is more emphasis on the income potential and management ability rather than on collateral security. It was pointed out that guidance and supervision are essential to an adequate rural credit program. It was also pointed out that loan repayment periods must be longer and flexible enough to meet the argicultural situation. Those are some of the principles which I suggest should be included in any public credit program.
Let me draw the minister's attention to the fact that one of the recommendations made was that the extension of loans for fixed and working capital by a farm credit lending agency should be done by one credit agency rather than a proliferation of agencies in order to permit sound supervision. Then they would be making a real contribution to the most basic of all industries in this country. They would not be adding to the costs of production that farmers face.

large a share of the capital market of the country and that by opening up the act the banks would be allowed to get into other fields and they might even be able to stay open longer. Now the government wants to reverse the process.

maintopic: LABOUR CONDITIONS-REQUEST FOR FAIR EMPLOYMENT PRACTICES LEGISLATION
LABOUR CONDITIONS-REQUEST FOR FAIR EMPLOYMENT PRACTICES LEGISLATION
speechtext:
A few days ago, Mr. Speaker, I asked the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mackasey) the following question, as reported at page 705 of Hansard:
In view of charges of sex discrimination in employment which were made yesterday by the president of the Canadian Labour Congress, and in view of the need to ensure that women workers will receive equal pay for comparable work and equal opportunity in respect of hiring and advancement, will the government consider the enactment of a fair employment practices act?
In reply the minister referred me to remarks made the previous evening by his parliamentary secretary. I looked up Hansard, Mr. Speaker, and found some references to the women's bureau and to the Female Employees Equal Pay Act. However, I found no reference whatever to a fair employment practices act. I am rather astonished that the Minister of Labour could so lightly dismiss the considered opinion of the president of a

October 7, 1968
large labour organization in this country which represents the overwhelming majority of the organized workers.
In speaking before the Royal Commission on the Status of Women, the president of the Canadian Labour Congress, as had the Canadian Union of Public Employees earlier, criticized the degree of discrimination against women workers. As a matter of fact, the president of the Canadian Labour Congress called for a fair employment commission which would, and I use his words, "forcibly and immediately eliminate discrimination against women on the job."
As I say, I have difficulty in understanding how the Minister of Labour could dismiss this matter in such a cursory manner. When we are speaking of discrimination against women workers in Canada, I think the minister would do well to remember that we are referring to one third of the Canadian labour force at the moment, and that is a very big segment indeed. Had he attended even one session of the Royal Commission on the Status of Women during the past week, he would have realized how deep and widespread is the resentment of women, and even some men in the Canadian congress, against this discrimination against women in our labour force.
This discrimination shows itself in a great many ways. For one thing, the labour congress made it clear that there is discrimination practised against women taking employment in traditionally male occupations. Consequently, these women are forced into occupations which are much less well paid and where frequently they are at the bottom of the pay scale. A newspaper article refers to the statement of the president of the Canadian Labour Congress this way:
Mr. MacDonald backed his case for the need to eliminate sex prejudice on the job by saying that jobs most frequently occupied by women, such as clerks, telephone operators, typists, hairdressers or launderers, seldom lead to advancement and are lower paid than areas where women do not predominate.
We might add that even in those industries where women predominate any males who may be working in it generally fare better financially.
We must remember that the vice president of the council of the Canadian Labour Congress met with Miss Hugette Plamondon, and we cannot forget her statement that when she looked at the pay schedule in a plant her heart started to pound because she realized that at the bottom of the pay scale would be the women workers.

Second, Mr Speaker, there is prejudice in women having positions of responsibility. Why? The usual excuses are given-that women are there for a short period only, that they cannot stand responsibility, and so on. I suspect that the males who got there first are being reluctant to share the more interesting work that responsibility entails, as well as the much better pay and undoubted status that goes with positions of responsibility.
Third, Mr Speaker, there is prejudice against women having supervisory positions over men or other women. Such a situation, which the minister dismissed so casually and briefly the other evening, violates both the United Nations universal declaration of human rights and also the I.L.O. convention respecting discrimination in respect of employment and occupation.
It is quite obvious, Mr. Speaker, from the testimony we heard last week before the commission that the Female Employees Equal Pay Act, which is administered by the women's bureau, has proved completely inadequate to deal with discrimination. The best proof of that fact is that the head of the women's bureau last spring quit her job in complete frustration. Simply paying a new supervisor of the women's bureau a higher salary is not going to get rid of the causes of frustration which brought about the resignation of the previous head. There is need-

speakeroldname: Mr. Jim McNulty (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Labour):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
maintopic: LABOUR CONDITIONS-REQUEST FOR FAIR EMPLOYMENT PRACTICES LEGISLATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have listened with a great deal of interest to the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway and, I must say, with a great deal of sympathy. Last week I explained that the Female Employees Equal Pay Act is basically good legislation and that its weakness rests with the fact that action can only be taken on complaints brought to our attention by affected workers. It is the intention of the Department of Labour to recommend that this act be amended so that the Department of Labour can act on its own initiative rather than on complaints, as is the present practice.
I also pointed out, as Mr. Little of the Canadian Union of Public Employees had already pointed out himself, that perhaps
October 7, 1968

sufficient efforts have not been made to acquaint women with this act and its provisions. Mr. Little was also frank and honest enough to indicate that the unions themselves are not without blame, a point substantiated by Miss Hugette Plamondon of the Canadian Labour Congress.
The Canadian Labour Congress has also referred to this problem in its brief to the Royal Commission on the Status of Women. No doubt the observations which have been made, particularly those concerning the interpretation of the terms "identical or substantially identical work", and the implementation of the act, will give rise to conclusions and recommendations by the commission.
With respect to equal opportunity in hiring and advancement, this is a very complex matter involving not only widespread social attitudes as to what is degrading work for women. The physical and mental health of women has also been protected by other laws which prohibit women from undertaking certain work. I have in mind legislation conforming with international labour conventions, such as the act prohibiting employment of women underground in mines.
[DOT] (10:10 p.m.)
When the grounds for discrimination were being established in our Canada Fair Employment Practices Act, it was decided that sex was not in the same category as colour, race, religion, or national origin. None of these bases have the slightest effect on employability or productivity in any occupation. However, there are many jobs requiring strengths usually associated with males, which most women could not fill, while there are other occupations, such as working underground in mines and the like, which society would deem unsuitable for women. There is also provincial legislation governing hours of work, rest periods, safety and health facilities provided in connection with employment of women as distinct from men. Experience has proven the need for legislation to protect women against hazards to which they are more vulnerable because of their sex.
In the case of the working mother for instance, limitations may actually facilitate her gainful employment, and preferential treatment must be expected when maternity conditions require her to take long periods off from work. In other words, because equitable terms of employment for women often require differentiation from those applied to men, sex is a quite different factor from the
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion other factors included in the Fair Employment Practices Act.
In the submission by the Canadian Labour Congress to the Royal Commission on the Status of Women, the congress recognizes there are broad social attitudes which could militate against the effectiveness of such legislation.
They state that prejudice against women taking employment in traditionally male occupations and against women being placed in supervisory positions over men, or even over other women, does not reside solely with management, but also extends to all levels of the employment structure.
