maintopic: DRUGS-INQUIRY AS TO ACTION TO CONTROL INCREASED NARCOTICS TRAFFIC
DRUGS-INQUIRY AS TO ACTION TO CONTROL INCREASED NARCOTICS TRAFFIC
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last Wednesday I asked the Minister of National Health and Welfare what his department is doing to educate young people to the dangers of taking drugs such as L.S.D., S.T.P. and heroin; whether serious consideration is being given to using communications techniques such as films, television programs and young people's popular magazines; and what research is being carried out to determine what long term effects these drugs have on people who use them, particularly on young people whose future could be ruined. It was suggested that this important question be placed on the order paper. Because of the importance of this subject I have asked for an opportunity to discuss it on the adjournment debate.
At the outset of my remarks I think I ought to bring something into perspective, and that is that I believe the vast majority of young people in Canada are not taking drugs and probably will never take drugs.

maintopic: DRUGS-INQUIRY AS TO ACTION TO CONTROL INCREASED NARCOTICS TRAFFIC
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: DRUGS-INQUIRY AS TO ACTION TO CONTROL INCREASED NARCOTICS TRAFFIC
speechtext:
But, Mr. Speaker, there are young people who are taking drugs such as L.S.D. and S.T.P., and there are others who can be influenced by them. All too often in recent months have we read and heard about L.S.D. and S.T.P. parties involving young people. We know of the many reasons our young people are turning to drugs, but the time allotted to me this evening does not permit my going into all the various aspects of the question. I should like to draw to Your
October 7, 19G8

Proceedings on Adjournment Motion Honour's attention one important reason, and that is ignorance. Our young people do not know how seriously they may endanger their physical and mental health as the result of just one experiment with L.S.D.
I should like to read what the Montreal Protestant School Board said recently in an effort to discourage student drug use:
We believe that only factual information well presented, and not conjecture based on emotional appeal, will have an influence on our young people today. The responsibility for communication of this information must be shared by educators, parents, students and the public at large.
This is a national problem and it must be treated as such. I maintain that this information should be initiated at the federal level. I do not think there is a town or community in this country which can sit back smugly and say: Drug addiction cannot happen here. Facts show that drug addiction can happen and does happen in many communities, and no one community or no one area is immune.
The Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Munro) said last week that he will be meeting with the provincial health ministers in the near future. I strongly urge that this subject be placed on the agenda and discussed. I urge the federal government to take the initiative in setting up an educational program in co-operation with the provinces. The money this program will cost will be money well spent.

speakeroldname: Mr. Robert Stanbury (Parliamentary Secretary to Secretary of State):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State of Canada
maintopic: DRUGS-INQUIRY AS TO ACTION TO CONTROL INCREASED NARCOTICS TRAFFIC
speechtext:
In the unavoidable absence of the Minister of National Health and Welfare and his parliamentary secretary I am glad to have the opportunity of congratulating the hon. member on his interest in this most important matter, an interest which I share both as a member of the standing committee on health and welfare in the last parliament and now as parliamentary secretary to the Secretary of State, who has a special concern for the youth of Canada.
The hon. member will know that under the terms of the British North America Act, there is no way in which the Department of National Health and Welfare can carry out an education program with respect to drug abuse or any other subject directly in the schools. What the department can do, and is doing, is to make informational materials available for use by school, community or other groups.
Some months ago officials of the department met with a group of high school teachers to discuss ways in which the department

could assist in informing young people of the dangers of drug abuse. As a result of this meeting the department has purchased a number of copies of a movie called "L.S.D.: Insight or Insanity" which it is making available to schools and other interested groups. As well, this film has been brought to the attention of the provincial departments of health and a number of these have ordered copies which they are making available within their respective provinces.
[DOT] (10:20 p.m.)
A number of publications dealing with L.S.D. and marijuana have been produced by the department in recent months and a major pamphlet, designed for mass distribution, is in its final stages of production. This pamphlet will be provided to provincial departments of health in sufficient quantity for distribution throughout the provinces.
It is the intention of the department to expand this informational program in every way possible in order to ensure that the consequences of the misuse of drugs are fully known to our young people.
As well, the department is continuing to reassess and update its control program as new hallucinogenic drugs come into use among young people. By order in council P.C. 1968-1736, Schedule H of the Food and Drug Act was amended last month by the addition of D.E.T., D.M.T. and S.T.P. This amendment will have the effect of prohibiting the sale of these substances as well as L.S.D. which was added to this schedule some time ago.
Item 29 in the list of bills presented to this house by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) on September 12, "A bill to amend the Food and Drug Act and the Narcotic Control Act and to make a consequential amendment to the Criminal Code," will further increase our capacity to control the use of hallucinogenic drugs. This bill will add to the Food and Drug Act an additional schedule to be known as restricted drugs and will provide penalties for possession, possession for purposes of trafficking, and trafficking in such substances as L.S.D., S.T.P. and other hallucinogenic drugs. maintopic: PUBLIC BUILDINGS-OTTAWA-COST OF NATIONAL ARTS CENTRE
PUBLIC BUILDINGS-OTTAWA-COST OF NATIONAL ARTS CENTRE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this afternoon I brought up the matter of the cost of the National Arts Centre which initially was not supposed to exceed $15 million. Yet, today, we are told that it will cost approximately $56 million.
I am happy to see the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Laing) in his seat tonight to take note of the brief remarks I will make on this matter.
In the Ottawa Journal of June 1966-over two years ago already-one could read this:

Contract for the main portion for the National Arts Centre today was awarded to V. K. Mason Construction of Ottawa on a $31,848,000 bid.
This brings the going price to date to $34,968,000.

And it is said that there is more. It is said now that there were three stages.
First stage:

Phase 1, the excavation, now complete and ready for superstructure, cost $1,453,000.
Phase 2, a portion of the underground garage with the job far from complete cost $1,667,000.
Phase 3, the construction of the three theatres, completion of underground parking and provision of facilities for restaurants, cafeterias, shopping mall, dressing rooms for 160 performers, rehearsal halls and administration offices now is scheduled to begin this July with a completion date set for January 1968.

The total amount at that time was supposed to reach approximately $35 million. That was in June 1966.

Awarding of contract was made public by Works Minister Mcllraith.

Mr. Speaker, recently, that is on October 3, we could read in the Ottawa Citizen the following:

Arts Centre cost now up to $46 million.
-Which means approximately. Reporter Greg Connolley said-

That means about $10 million more than the amount mentioned two years ago.
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion
That is what prompted Mr. Greg Connolly, of the press gallery, to say, when he questioned certain members, including the former prime minister of Canada, the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker), and I quote:

His eyebrows almost popped out of sight when he noted the cost for furniture in the centre was not set at $3,989,000.

We are speaking of $4 million, for furniture only, which prompted the former prime minister to say:

"They must be getting that place dressed up like Joe Greene's office."

Mr. Speaker, there is something abnormal here. Those contracts were given after tenders had been submitted. Now, after the tenders have been received, the contract given, here we are-two years later-with increases of $10, $12 and $15 million. Why tender then, if it serves no purpose?
If someone agrees to do a job for $31 million, how is it that two years later we have a $46 million undertaking? How come $15 million have been added? Is that fair to the other tenderers? Is it fair to the Canadian people who witness such a scandal?
Without the shadow of a doubt, in the minds of the Canadian people, there is messing around somewhere, probably with the election funds, where the contractors are concerned.
We are not against the construction of the Arts Centre; far from it.
Even a Liberal member, the other day, complained about the way the walls of the Arts Centre look.
Mr. Speaker, tenders are submitted and a contract is given to a contractor only after a department has inquired into his financial situation. If the contractor is not solvent, he is not given the contract.
Mr. Speaker, the situation with regard to the construction of the Arts Centre in Ottawa is inexplicable. That is why 1 put a question about it to the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) this afternoon. Since the Minister of Public Works is now in the house, I ask him to tell us why the Canadian people should pay $56 million. I am not the one to say that; it was said by the experts who figured the cost of the Ottawa Arts Centre.
October 7, 1963

Proceedings on Adjournment Motion
This centre will cost $56 million, instead of $15 or $20 millions as provided. What portion of that amount of $56 million went to financing the election of the government in office? What amount was provided by the Mason Construction, by subcontractors, such as Pitt's for instance, who was supposed to do the excavation? Architects also were involved. The Foundation of Canada built the garage. The Spino Construction built the tunnel which costs over half a million dollars.
Mr. Speaker, it might be a good idea to tell the Canadian people, and especially the house, what are the reasons for a price increase such as we witness at the present time.

speakeroldname: Mr. Robert Stanbury (Parliamentary Secretary to Secretary of State):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State of Canada
maintopic: PUBLIC BUILDINGS-OTTAWA-COST OF NATIONAL ARTS CENTRE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if I heard the hon. member correctly he mentioned a figure of $56 million. As a citizen of Ontario who has watched the mushrooming cost of the provincial science and technology centre in Toronto, I sympathize with him, but I do not think he should make the matter worse than it is. Perhaps he was dealing in Social Credit dollars. The government's estimate for completing the national arts centre is $46,426,000.
The figure of $9 million with which some comparison has been made was produced in October 1963 by a group of private citizens who called themselves the national capital arts alliance. This figure was contained in a submission they made to the government recommending the construction of an arts centre.
At that stage they were expressing a desire for a centre to contain provision for opera and an experimental studio, and their estimates were based on prices of previously constructed single unit theatres. No site had been selected although they did recommend a site at Sussex and St. Patrick streets which was relatively open and they believed surface parking would be available. No detailed study had been made on the development of the type of facilities they wished the centre to include. They estimated that the building would contain 4.8 million cubic feet with a floor area of 175,000 square feet.
The project which the government has built is an entirely different project. It contains 16 million cubic feet of space with a floor area of 924,000 square feet including a 900 vehicle underground parking garage.
As part of the development of the capital area it has been constructed on Confederation square, and while in this location it contributes to our capital, its location involves foundation conditions and the necessity of constructing a major portion below ground, as well as the provision of substantial changes in the routing of traffic and access tunnels to the parking, none of which was contemplated by the original proposers of the scheme.
[DOT] (10:30 p.m.)
The government approved of the project in a general sense in February of 1964 with the decision to accept the city owned portion of the Confederation square site and set up advisory committees to determine the requirements in providing facilities for opera, music, theatre and visual arts. These committees have developed the requirements so that the centre will provide for the total range of performing arts under first class conditions, of which Canada as a whole will be justifiably proud. The cost of the construction elements of the centre is $38,922,000 with the parking garage a $3,606,000, these figures including the cost of the necessary relocation and provision of services, such as power, water, telephone and streets. Then $3,898,000 will be spent on theatre equipment and furnishings.
The construction has been in four phases; a preliminary excavation contract being awarded in January, 1965, construction of the Mackenzie King bridge approach and a portion of the garage in June 1965, a tunnel entrance under Elgin street in August 1966, with the major theatre construction contract being awarded in June, 1966. Work on the centre is progressing and will be complete in order that the first performance may take place in June, 1969.
